Real-World Applications Aerospace: Turbine blades, engine parts, structural components Medical Devices: Surgical instruments, precision implants Automotive: Engine components, chassis parts, brackets Electronics & Consumer Products: Enclosures, housings, intricate components Furniture & Woodworking: Custom designs with complex curves and surfaces CNC machining excels in high-precision, repeatable applications, while manual machining is still used for simple or custom jobs where human skill is critical. Best Practices for Choosing Between CNC and Manual Project Scale: Large batches favor CNC; one-offs may favor manual. Complexity & Precision: CNC handles complex, high-tolerance designs better. Material Selection: CNC supports a wider range of materials with minimal setup. Budget & Time: CNC requires higher upfront investment but saves time and costs in production runs. Environment & Resources: Consider operator skill, machine availability, and workflow integration. FAQs Q1: Is CNC better than manual for prototypes? A: For simple one-off parts, manual machining may be faster. For precise or complex prototypes, CNC is preferable. Q2: Can CNC handle all types of materials? A: CNC machines handle metals, plastics, and composites, though tooling and cutting parameters must be adjusted per material. Q3: Is small-batch CNC production economical? A: Yes. JLCCNC offers small-batch CNC services starting from $1, making it cost-effective even for low volumes. Q4: Which method is faster? A: CNC is faster for medium to large runs or complex parts. Manual machining can be faster for very simple or urgent one-off tasks. Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals CNC Machining vs. Rapid Prototyping When to Combine Both Technologies Published null, updated Apr 28, 2025 5 min CNC machining (CNC) and rapid prototyping (RP) are two disruptive technologies in the manufacturing industry, the former for high precision and volume production, the latter for rapid prototyping and complex structure forming. However, many organisations face confusion when choosing a technology path: when should either technology be used alone? When do you need to combine the two to achieve synergistic effects? In this paper, we will analyse the complementary nature of the two technologies from the technical characteristics, applicable scenarios and integration strategies to help you optimize the manufacturing process and reduce costs. I. Comparison of CNC Machining and Rapid Prototyping Technologies 1. CNC machining: synonymous with precision and stability Technical characteristics: through digital programming control tool movement, metal, plastic and other materials cutting, milling and drilling, precision up to ± 0.01mm, surface roughness as low as Ra0.2μm. Advantage: suitable for mass production, high-precision parts (such as engine block, mould cavity) and complex surface processing (such as automotive cover parts). Limitations: high cost of moulds in the early stage, long cycle of small batch trial production, and difficult processing of complex internal cavity structure. 2. Rapid prototyping: an innovative tool for agility and freedom Technical characteristics: based on the principle of layered superposition, through 3D printing, laser sintering (SLS), fused deposition (FDM) and other ways to directly generate a solid model, without the need for moulds, the material utilization rate is close to 100%. Advantage: Suitable for single piece/small batch prototyping (e.g. concept car shells), complex skeleton structures (e.g. lightweight aerospace parts) and rapid mould manufacturing. Limitations: Limited material properties (e.g. strength, temperature resistance), high surface roughness (Ra3.2μm or more), high cost of mass production. 3. Comparison Summary Dimension CNC Machining Rapid prototyping Precision Sub-millimetre (±0.01mm) Millimetre grade (±0.1mm) Cost-effectiveness Highly economical for large quantities Excellent economy for small lot sizes Design Freedom Limited by tools and fixtures Supports any complex geometry Material range Metal, engineering plastics mainly Resin, nylon, metal powder, ceramics, etc. II. 4 Typical Scenarios of When to Combine Two Technologies 1. Staged manufacturing of complex parts Case: aerospace engine turbine blades Rapid prototyping: first use SLS technology to print wax prototypes with complex cooling channels to verify aerodynamic performance. CNC machining: Combined with the investment casting process, the casting cavity is refined by CNC to ensure that the surface finish of the blade reaches Ra0.4μm. Advantage: Shorten the development cycle by 30% and reduce the cost of trial and error by 50%. 2. Hybrid manufacturing of rapid moulds Case: automotive interior injection mould Rapid prototyping: make paper master mould through LOM technology to quickly verify the mould structure. CNC machining: Using the master mould as a reference, use 5-axis CNC to machine the steel mould core with an accuracy of ±0.02mm. Advantage: Mould delivery cycle is shortened from 3 months to 3 weeks. 3. Functional enhancement of functional prototypes Case: Medical device metal implant Rapid prototyping: Manufacture of porous osseointegrated structures using metal 3D printing (e.g. SLM). CNC machining: CNC finishing of critical contact surfaces (e.g. threaded holes) with roughness optimised to Ra0.8μm. Advantage: balance between biocompatibility and mechanical strength, FDA-approved efficiency increased by 40%. 4. Small-lot customised production Case: High-end customised watch case Rapid prototyping: Rapid production of personalised design prototypes using light-curing (SLA) technology. CNC machining: Titanium alloy case is machined by precision mill-turn machine with tolerance control of ±0.005mm. Advantage: Customers only need 10 days from design to delivery, and the premium ability is increased by 30%. III. 3 Core Strategies for Technology Integration 1. Data chain synergy: seamless connection from CAD to CAM Method: Realise design model directly drive RP and CNC equipment through unified software platform (e.g. UG, MasterCAM) to avoid format conversion error. Value: Reduce repeated modelling time by 60% and reduce the risk of human error. 2. Material and process matching Metal field: RP manufacture near-net shape blank, CNC complete high-precision cutting (such as aluminium alloy impeller). Plastic: FDM printing functional prototypes, CNC machining glass fibre reinforced nylon jigs and fixtures. 3. Cost and efficiency balance Economy formula: Total cost = (RP cost × quantity) + (CNC cost × finishing ratio) When the batch size <50 pieces, the priority is RP + CNC hybrid solution; when the batch size >500 pieces, CNC independent production is more advantageous. IV. JLCCNC: CNC and rapid prototyping integration of manufacturing leaders JLCCNC specializes in the field of precision manufacturing, providing CNC machining and rapid prototyping synergistic solutions for automotive, aerospace, medical and other industries. Successful case: Developed battery tray for a new energy vehicle enterprise, 3D printing lightweight structure + CNC high-precision sealing surface machining, 15% weight reduction and 20% cost reduction. Helped a medical device company to achieve mass production of customised hip implants, reducing lead time by 50%. Contact JLCCNC today to unlock the unlimited possibilities of CNC and additive manufacturing! How to E-Coat CNC Parts Why E-Coating Is Gaining Popularity What Is E-Coating? E-coating , short for electrophoretic coating , is a high-performance finishing technique widely used in CNC manufacturing, especially for metal components. It involves applying a protective and decorative paint-like layer using an electrically charged bath. Think of it like electroplating, but with paint particles instead of metal ions. The result? A thin, uniform, corrosion-resistant layer that coats even the hardest-to-reach corners of complex CNC-machined parts. If you're wondering “what is e coating and why should I care?”. Here's why: it combines the efficiency of powder coating with the smooth finish of wet paint, offering outstanding durability and coverage for automotive, aerospace, electronics, and industrial machinery components. How Does the E-Coating Process Work? Let’s break down the e coating process step-by-step: 1. Cleaning & Pretreatment CNC machined parts are thoroughly cleaned to remove oils, dirt, and machining residue. This step is crucial, contaminants affect adhesion. 2. Phosphate Conversion Coating (Optional) For steel and some aluminum parts, a phosphate layer may be applied to improve paint adhesion and corrosion resistance. 3. E-Coating Tank (Electrophoresis) Here’s where the magic happens. The parts are submerged in a tank containing water-based paint particles suspended in solution. When an electrical current is applied: ○ The paint particles migrate toward the part (cathode or anode, depending on the process). ○ They form a uniform coating layer that clings tightly to every surface. 4. Rinsing Excess coating is rinsed off to prevent uneven buildup. 5. Curing/Baking The part is baked at 150 - 200°C. This crosslinks the coating, hardens it, and locks it in. E-Coating vs Powder Coating A common debate in surface finishing: e coating vs powder coating . Both provide excellent protection, but they serve slightly different purposes. Feature E-Coating Powder Coating Application Method Submersion + electric charge Electrostatic spray gun Coverage Excellent in complex geometries Great for flat or open surfaces Coating Thickness Thin, highly uniform Thicker, may not reach tight crevices Appearance Smooth, consistent Can have orange peel effect Corrosion Resistance High Very high with thicker layers Best for Priming, complex parts, CNC internal cavities Decorative finishes, exterior applications Takeaway : Use e-coating when part complexity and internal protection matter most. Powder coating excels in aesthetic appeal and surface durability. If you're exploring advanced finishes like e-coating or need precision CNC machining for functional prototypes or production parts, our team delivers consistent, high-quality results tailored to your specs. Get a quote today . Applications of E-Coating in CNC Machining CNC machined components that benefit from e-coating include: ● Steel brackets and enclosures (especially for electrical/electronic systems) ● Precision aluminum housings ● Complex automotive frames or mounts ● Fasteners, springs, and gears ● Medical and lab equipment requiring sterile, coated surfaces The appeal lies in its pin-hole-free, even coverage , even on intricate geometries that traditional spraying misses. To better understand how different surface finishes like e-coating impact the performance and durability of CNC-machined components, check out our detailed guide on the role of surface finish in CNC machining. E-Coating vs Anodizing Both are thin-film protective processes, but here’s how they differ. Feature E-Coating Anodizing Base Metals Supported Steel, aluminum, others Primarily aluminum and titanium Coating Material Paint/resin Oxide layer grown from the metal itself Color Options Wide (via pigments) Limited without dyeing Wear Resistance Moderate (depends on resin) Excellent, especially Type III anodizing Electrical Conductivity Insulating Varies (can be reduced but not fully lost) E-coating is more universal and versatile in color/appearance. Anodizing is better for aluminum and superior abrasion resistance. Can E-Coating Be Used With Electronic Nickel Plating? Yes, electronic nickel plating (ENP) is often applied before e-coating for dual protection: ● ENP gives wear resistance and hardness (ideal for CNC parts in high-friction environments). ● E-coating adds corrosion protection and a decorative surface. This combo is especially useful in aerospace and automotive , where both friction and environmental exposure are concerns. How to E-Coat CNC Parts While the equipment and chemistry are specialized, here’s a simplified breakdown of how to e coat in a production setting: 1. Design your part with coating in mind, no deep blind holes that trap solutions. 2. Choose your material , steel and aluminum are ideal. 3. Send parts to an e-coating facility (not typically done in-house for low volumes). 4. The facility will perform the multi-stage cleaning, coating, curing , and quality control. If you're considering integrating e-coating into your production pipeline, make sure your CNC service provider offers tight tolerance machining that accounts for post-processing thickness. Why E-Coating Is Gaining Popularity Some reasons e-coating is becoming a go-to in modern CNC manufacturing: ● Eco-Friendly : Low VOCs, water-based solutions ● Repeatable : Automated process ensures consistency ● Cost-Effective : Lower material waste compared to spraying ● Tight Tolerance Friendly : Minimal material buildup (often 15 - 25 microns) Need precision CNC parts ready for surface finishing like e-coating? Our CNC machining services offer ultra-clean finishes, tight tolerances, and production-ready parts that are ideal for post-processing, including e-coating, anodizing, powder coating, and more. Limitations to Consider EDM Hole Drilling Machines: What Makes Them Special? Want Extreme Accuracy? EDM Might Be the Way Drilling a hole sounds simple, until you need to do it with extreme precision, into hardened materials, or to microscopic depths. That’s when you start comparing EDM hole drilling and conventional CNC drilling side by side. While both are designed to create holes, their technologies, capabilities, and ideal use cases couldn’t be more different. So, which method should you choose for your next project? Let’s dig in. What Is EDM Hole Drilling? EDM (Electrical Discharge Machining) hole drilling , also called hole popping EDM or EDM deep hole drilling , uses electrical sparks to erode material. Instead of a rotating drill bit, it uses a tubular electrode and dielectric fluid to remove metal through high-frequency discharges. It’s a non-contact process, meaning the tool doesn’t make direct physical contact with the material during machining. The result? It can drill extremely precise, burr-free holes even in hardened steel, carbides, or exotic alloys . What Is Conventional CNC Hole Drilling? CNC hole drilling uses rotating cutting tools<dynamic-value> twist drills or end mills, to cut into material. It's what most people imagine when they think about machining a hole. From high-speed spindles to peck drilling cycles, CNC machines are versatile and fast, especially when you're working with softer materials or mass production. But it’s still a contact-based process , and precision can degrade with wear, heat, or vibration. EDM vs Drilling: The Core Differences Feature EDM Hole Drilling CNC Drilling Material Type Conductive materials only (e.g., steel, titanium) Any machinable material Tool Contact No physical contact Direct contact via tool Hole Size Micro to medium (0.1 mm to 6 mm) Wide range (0.5 mm to 50+ mm) Tolerance Extremely tight (±0.002 mm possible) Moderate (±0.05 mm typical) Hole Depth Excellent for deep, narrow holes (30:1+ depth-to-diameter) Limited by tool rigidity and chip evacuation Speed Slower Faster for larger holes Surface Finish Very smooth, no burrs May require deburring or finishing Tool Wear Minimal due to no mechanical contact High, especially in hard materials Are you unsure about which process is right for your metal part? We can help you choose the most precise and cost-effective method for your job. Get a free quote here and let's make your design manufacturable. When to Use EDM Hole Drilling The EDM hole drilling process shines in high-precision, small-diameter, deep-hole situations, especially where conventional drilling fails or causes tool breakage. Use cases include: ● Turbine blades (for cooling holes) ● Fuel injector nozzles ● Aerospace components ● Medical devices requiring micro holes ● Hard tool steels or materials like Inconel and titanium Also, EDM is ideal when you need starter holes for wire EDM , which conventional tools can’t drill due to hardness or geometry. When to Use Conventional CNC Drilling For general-purpose hole making in aluminum, plastics, or mild steel, CNC hole drilling is faster and more cost-effective. Use cases include: ● Bolt holes, pilot holes, tapped holes ● Large hole drilling in brackets or frames ● Machining production parts in batches ● Applications where tight tolerance is not critical And yes, to answer a common question, can a CNC machine drill holes? Absolutely. In fact, it’s one of the most common operations in any CNC shop. EDM Holes vs Drilled Holes: What About Quality? EDM holes tend to be cleaner and burr-free straight off the machine. Their surface finish is smoother, with no mechanical stress or deformation around the hole. This makes them ideal for critical applications where dimensional stability and fatigue resistance matter. CNC-drilled holes, on the other hand, often need secondary processes , like deburring or reaming, to meet similar tolerances and finishes, especially in small diameters or deep holes. Limitations to Consider While EDM hole drilling offers unmatched precision, it’s not ideal for every scenario . ● It can’t be used on non-conductive materials (like plastic or glass). ● It’s relatively slow for large-diameter holes. ● Machines and electrodes are more expensive and require specialized operators. Conversely, CNC drilling tools wear faster in hardened materials, and the deeper you go, the higher the risk of tool deflection, chatter, or breakage . EDM Hole Drilling Machines: What Makes Them Special? A dedicated hole drilling EDM machine is typically compact, automated, and capable of producing holes as small as 0.1 mm in tough metals. Many come with automatic electrode changers and multi-axis positioning. For shops working with aerospace, mold making, or die sinking, having one on the floor is a game-changer for precision parts. Want Extreme Accuracy? EDM Might Be the Way If you're prototyping intricate components or producing parts where one imperfect hole can ruin the entire build , go for EDM. But if you’re running production batches, drilling aluminum brackets, or cutting costs, CNC drilling is often more practical. Choose the Right Tool for the Hole Not every hole is created equal, and neither are the tools that make them. Whether you choose EDM hole drilling for ultra-precision or CNC hole drilling for speed and efficiency, understanding their strengths is the first step toward better manufacturing outcomes. If you’re unsure what your application calls for, talk to your machinist, or even better, partner with a shop that offers both options . Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals The Three Types of EDM Machining and How They Differ Published Jan 11, 2024, updated Aug 21, 2026 6 min Table of Contents What is and why do we use Electric Discharge Machining Materials and Applications in EDM Machining Differences between these three techniques Conclusion What is and why do we use Electric Discharge Machining EDM, or Electrical Discharge Machining, serves as a substitute for traditional machining methods when dealing with tough materials, particularly refractory metals and intricate shapes that are challenging to cut. Wire EDM enables the attainment of precision cuts with tolerances that would otherwise be unachievable, while hole drilling EDM excels in achieving precise diameters and roundness. Overall, EDM ensures exceptional precision and exceptionally low Ra levels, resulting in high-quality surface finishes. This characteristic reduces the need for extensive post-processing, ultimately lowering costs associated with manufacturing components that are notoriously difficult to produce. Technique 1: Hole Drilling EDM Hole Drilling EDM, also known as EDM Hole Drilling or EDM Micro-Drilling, is a specialized variant of Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM). We specifically designed it to create precise and accurate holes in various materials, including metals and alloys. In Hole Drilling EDM, a small-diameter electrode, typically a rotating brass or copper tube, is used to generate a series of rapid electrical discharges. These discharges occur between the electrode and the workpiece, creating controlled erosion and gradually drilling a hole through the material. The process involves flushing a dielectric fluid, such as deionized water, through the electrode to flush away debris and cool the workpiece. The dielectric fluid also acts as a conductor for the electrical discharges. We value hole Drilling EDM for its ability to create highly accurate holes with tight tolerances, even in materials that are difficult to machine using conventional drilling methods. It is commonly used in industries such as aerospace, medical, automotive, and electronics, where precision holes are required for applications like cooling channels, fuel injection nozzles, or turbine blades. Technique 2: Sinker Discharge Machining Electrical discharge machining (EDM) is a type of procedure used for shaping and machining conductive materials. We refer it to as sinker discharge machining, sinker EDM, or conventional EDM. In Sinker Discharge Machining, a tool called a "sinker electrode" is used, which is typically made of graphite or copper. It shaped the sinker electrode to match the desired form or cavity that needs to be created in the workpiece. The process involves placing the sinker electrode close to the workpiece, with a dielectric fluid, such as oil or deionized water, acting as a medium between them. A series of electrical discharges, or sparks, are generated between the sinker electrode and the workpiece. These electrical discharges create controlled erosion, gradually removing material from the workpiece and shaping it according to the geometry of the sinker electrode. Sinker Release Intricate and complicated forms, such as molds, dies, and tooling components, are frequently made using machining. Because it does not need mechanical effort and doesn't create any noticeable heat-affected zones, it works especially well for cutting tough materials. Sinker EDM is capable of high accuracy and precise surface finishes, making it suited for sectors such as aerospace, automotive, tool and die manufacture, and medical device manufacturing. Technique 3: Wire Cut EDM Wire Cut EDM, also known as Wire Electrical Discharge Machining or Wire EDM, is a specialized kind of Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) used for the precision cutting and shaping of conductive materials. A sequence of electrical discharges, or sparks, between the wire and the workpiece, are produced throughout the operation. The substance melts and evaporates because of the controlled erosion produced by these electrical discharges. The wire advances continuously, guaranteeing a continuous cutting action and enabling the machining of intricate forms and curves. Tight tolerances may be achieved, and wire-cut EDM is highly accurate. Cutting complex forms, thin sections, and contours in a variety of materials, such as metals, alloys, and conductive ceramics, is a popular use for it. Producing dies, molds, and tooling components for the precise engineering, automotive, aerospace, and electronics sectors is very helpful. Wire Cut EDM offers advantages, such as the ability to cut materials regardless of their hardness, minimal heat-affected zones, and the ability to achieve fine surface finishes. It is a flexible machining technique that allows for the high repeatability manufacturing of intricate and accurate components. Materials and Applications in EDM Machining EDM primarily handles materials that pose challenges for conventional machining methods, including tungsten, molybdenum, and hardened tool steels. Additionally, materials like titanium and austenitic stainless steels, which demonstrate significant work hardening during mechanical machining processes, are well-suited for EDM. As these materials harden while being machined, they become increasingly difficult to cut. Consequently, this hardening phenomenon often leads to a reduction in the accuracy of the machined part features. Electric discharge machining finds application in the production of molds for plastic injection molding and metal die casting. It is utilized to create intricate cavities in pre-hardened materials, showcasing its proficiency in achieving precise and complex cavity shapes, as well as executing deep cuts. Industries such as aerospace, automobile, and electronics also rely on EDM for fabricating prototypes and manufacturing various components. Differences between these three techniques Different types of EDM are classified based on their operations and applications. One example is wire EDM, which utilizes a linear feed wire electrode to make primarily two-dimensional cuts. We position the electrode wire on a guide made of diamond or sapphire, and the dielectric fluid used is typically deionized water. Brass or galvanized brass is commonly employed for the electrode material. In contrast, sinker discharge EDM allows for the utilization of intricate electrode shapes to create equally complex cavities. Graphite or copper electrodes are pre-machined into the desired shape and then eroded into the workpiece, resulting in holes that mirror the shape of the electrode. Drilling EDM is capable of producing smaller and deeper holes compared to traditional drilling methods. This enables precise diameters, roundness, excellent surface finishes, and eliminates burrs. Electrodes in drilling EDM can have intricate cross-sectional shapes. Drill tools often incorporate cooling channels through which dielectric fluid is circulated to aid in the removal of chips. Sinker discharge machining stands out as the most suitable type of EDM for fabricating components with intricate cavities. It enables the creation of complex cavity shapes frequently needed in the design of plastic and die-cast parts. While there are limitations to the range of cavity shapes achievable through sinker discharge EDM, these restrictions do not significantly affect its effectiveness as a tool for mold-making. The concept of the "line of the draw," which restricts EDM from producing undercuts, also applies to plastic molded and die-cast parts. These parts enter the tool cavity in liquid form but solidify as they exit. Conclusion To conclude, this article described the many forms of EDM machining, their differences, and when to utilize them. Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals The Three Types of EDM Machining and How They Differ Published Jan 11, 2024, updated Aug 21, 2026 6 min Table of Contents What is and why do we use Electric Discharge Machining Materials and Applications in EDM Machining Differences between these three techniques Conclusion What is and why do we use Electric Discharge Machining EDM, or Electrical Discharge Machining, serves as a substitute for traditional machining methods when dealing with tough materials, particularly refractory metals and intricate shapes that are challenging to cut. Wire EDM enables the attainment of precision cuts with tolerances that would otherwise be unachievable, while hole drilling EDM excels in achieving precise diameters and roundness. Overall, EDM ensures exceptional precision and exceptionally low Ra levels, resulting in high-quality surface finishes. This characteristic reduces the need for extensive post-processing, ultimately lowering costs associated with manufacturing components that are notoriously difficult to produce. Technique 1: Hole Drilling EDM Hole Drilling EDM, also known as EDM Hole Drilling or EDM Micro-Drilling, is a specialized variant of Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM). We specifically designed it to create precise and accurate holes in various materials, including metals and alloys. In Hole Drilling EDM, a small-diameter electrode, typically a rotating brass or copper tube, is used to generate a series of rapid electrical discharges. These discharges occur between the electrode and the workpiece, creating controlled erosion and gradually drilling a hole through the material. The process involves flushing a dielectric fluid, such as deionized water, through the electrode to flush away debris and cool the workpiece. The dielectric fluid also acts as a conductor for the electrical discharges. We value hole Drilling EDM for its ability to create highly accurate holes with tight tolerances, even in materials that are difficult to machine using conventional drilling methods. It is commonly used in industries such as aerospace, medical, automotive, and electronics, where precision holes are required for applications like cooling channels, fuel injection nozzles, or turbine blades. Technique 2: Sinker Discharge Machining Electrical discharge machining (EDM) is a type of procedure used for shaping and machining conductive materials. We refer it to as sinker discharge machining, sinker EDM, or conventional EDM. In Sinker Discharge Machining, a tool called a "sinker electrode" is used, which is typically made of graphite or copper. It shaped the sinker electrode to match the desired form or cavity that needs to be created in the workpiece. The process involves placing the sinker electrode close to the workpiece, with a dielectric fluid, such as oil or deionized water, acting as a medium between them. A series of electrical discharges, or sparks, are generated between the sinker electrode and the workpiece. These electrical discharges create controlled erosion, gradually removing material from the workpiece and shaping it according to the geometry of the sinker electrode. Sinker Release Intricate and complicated forms, such as molds, dies, and tooling components, are frequently made using machining. Because it does not need mechanical effort and doesn't create any noticeable heat-affected zones, it works especially well for cutting tough materials. Sinker EDM is capable of high accuracy and precise surface finishes, making it suited for sectors such as aerospace, automotive, tool and die manufacture, and medical device manufacturing. Technique 3: Wire Cut EDM Wire Cut EDM, also known as Wire Electrical Discharge Machining or Wire EDM, is a specialized kind of Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) used for the precision cutting and shaping of conductive materials. A sequence of electrical discharges, or sparks, between the wire and the workpiece, are produced throughout the operation. The substance melts and evaporates because of the controlled erosion produced by these electrical discharges. The wire advances continuously, guaranteeing a continuous cutting action and enabling the machining of intricate forms and curves. Tight tolerances may be achieved, and wire-cut EDM is highly accurate. Cutting complex forms, thin sections, and contours in a variety of materials, such as metals, alloys, and conductive ceramics, is a popular use for it. Producing dies, molds, and tooling components for the precise engineering, automotive, aerospace, and electronics sectors is very helpful. Wire Cut EDM offers advantages, such as the ability to cut materials regardless of their hardness, minimal heat-affected zones, and the ability to achieve fine surface finishes. It is a flexible machining technique that allows for the high repeatability manufacturing of intricate and accurate components. Materials and Applications in EDM Machining EDM primarily handles materials that pose challenges for conventional machining methods, including tungsten, molybdenum, and hardened tool steels. Additionally, materials like titanium and austenitic stainless steels, which demonstrate significant work hardening during mechanical machining processes, are well-suited for EDM. As these materials harden while being machined, they become increasingly difficult to cut. Consequently, this hardening phenomenon often leads to a reduction in the accuracy of the machined part features. Electric discharge machining finds application in the production of molds for plastic injection molding and metal die casting. It is utilized to create intricate cavities in pre-hardened materials, showcasing its proficiency in achieving precise and complex cavity shapes, as well as executing deep cuts. Industries such as aerospace, automobile, and electronics also rely on EDM for fabricating prototypes and manufacturing various components. Differences between these three techniques Different types of EDM are classified based on their operations and applications. One example is wire EDM, which utilizes a linear feed wire electrode to make primarily two-dimensional cuts. We position the electrode wire on a guide made of diamond or sapphire, and the dielectric fluid used is typically deionized water. Brass or galvanized brass is commonly employed for the electrode material. In contrast, sinker discharge EDM allows for the utilization of intricate electrode shapes to create equally complex cavities. Graphite or copper electrodes are pre-machined into the desired shape and then eroded into the workpiece, resulting in holes that mirror the shape of the electrode. Drilling EDM is capable of producing smaller and deeper holes compared to traditional drilling methods. This enables precise diameters, roundness, excellent surface finishes, and eliminates burrs. Electrodes in drilling EDM can have intricate cross-sectional shapes. Drill tools often incorporate cooling channels through which dielectric fluid is circulated to aid in the removal of chips. Sinker discharge machining stands out as the most suitable type of EDM for fabricating components with intricate cavities. It enables the creation of complex cavity shapes frequently needed in the design of plastic and die-cast parts. While there are limitations to the range of cavity shapes achievable through sinker discharge EDM, these restrictions do not significantly affect its effectiveness as a tool for mold-making. The concept of the "line of the draw," which restricts EDM from producing undercuts, also applies to plastic molded and die-cast parts. These parts enter the tool cavity in liquid form but solidify as they exit. Conclusion To conclude, this article described the many forms of EDM machining, their differences, and when to utilize them. Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals What is Face Milling: Process, tools and operation Published Jun 13, 2025, updated Jun 19, 2025 7 min Table of Contents What Is Face Milling? How the Face Milling Process Works Common Face Milling Tools Types of Face Milling Operations Best Practices for Cleaner Face Milling Master the Cut Before You Hit Cycle Start Face milling doesn’t get the spotlight much, but it’s one of those workhorse processes that keeps machining shops running smooth. If you’ve ever needed a flat surface that’s actually flat , you’ve relied on it, whether you realized it or not. So what exactly is face milling? Think of it as the process behind every perfectly squared metal block, every smooth aluminum plate, every clean surface that just feels right. It’s precise, fast, and oddly satisfying to watch. But it’s not just about spinning a tool across some metal. The cutter design, tool path, speeds, and setup all play a role in getting that crisp finish without wrecking your inserts or your workpiece. In this guide, we’re breaking down how face milling works, what tools you’ll need, the types of operations involved, and a few tips that’ll save your cutters, and your sanity. What Is Face Milling? (istock) Face milling is one of the most common, and most essential, processes in the machining world. It’s all about cutting a flat surface perpendicular to the tool’s axis, usually with a wide face mill cutter that skims across the top of the material. The result? A smooth, level finish that’s ready for the next operation. Unlike side milling , which cuts along the edge or profile of a part, face milling focuses on creating a clean, wide face. It’s often the first step in squaring up a workpiece or prepping raw stock in a facing milling machine . What makes it effective is the tool design. A face mill tool typically uses multiple cutting edges (inserts) mounted in a circular holder. These inserts do most of the work, shaving off material in fast, controlled passes. You’ll find face mills in CNC shops, manual mills, and production floors alike, especially where consistency and finish quality matter. How the Face Milling Process Works The concept is simple: a rotating face mill sweeps across the surface of your material, cutting with the edges on the bottom of the tool. The setup, however, is where the real work begins. In a typical operation, the facing mill is mounted in a vertical spindle. As it spins, the inserts take shallow bites out of the material with each pass. The machine feeds the workpiece horizontally while the tool keeps cutting, layer by layer. It’s fast, consistent, and perfect for prepping a surface for tight-tolerance parts. The results depend on your setup, feed rate, cutting speed, tool path, and depth of cut all play a role. A roughing pass might take off more material quickly, while a finishing pass uses a finer face milling cutter for that clean, reflective finish. Tool rigidity and part stability matter. If your setup flexes, the finish suffers. If your inserts are dull, you’ll get chatter and uneven cuts. It's the kind of job where details make all the difference, and a decent face milling machine won't cover for poor planning. Roughing vs Finishing Parameter Roughing Finishing Depth of Cut 2–5 mm (0.08–0.2 in) 0.2–1 mm (0.01–0.04 in) Feed Rate Higher (aggressive) Lower (controlled) Cutting Speed Moderate Higher Tool Used Indexable face mill Fly cutter / fine-tooth mill Surface Finish Coarse Smooth (low Ra value) Common Face Milling Tools There’s more than one way to flatten a surface, and the tool you pick makes a big difference on your finish, your cycle time, and your tooling cost. Let’s break down the most common options used in face milling . Tool Selection Guide: When to Use What Tool Type Best For Pros Cons Face Mill Cutter General purpose, roughing + finishing Fast, efficient, easy insert swap Higher upfront cost Shell Mill Large parts, modular setups Versatile, scalable Needs arbor and holder setup Fly Cutter Finishing small to medium surfaces Inexpensive, smooth finish Slow, can vibrate at high speeds Solid Carbide Tool Light machines, tight spaces Rigid, compact Pricey, limited insert options Types of Face Milling Operations (ResearchGate) Face milling isn’t just about plowing a tool across a block of metal. There are different ways to run the cut, and knowing the options helps you get better results, or avoid screwing things up. Conventional Face Milling This is your go-to method. The face mill cuts across the entire top of the workpiece, removing material in overlapping passes. It’s efficient and ideal for prepping flat surfaces quickly. Partial Face Milling When the workpiece is smaller or has tricky geometry, only part of the face milling cutter engages with the material. It requires a bit more care in setup to avoid deflection and uneven cuts. Climb vs. Conventional Milling In climb milling, the cutter moves in the same direction as the feed, great finish, but it needs a solid machine. Conventional milling moves against the feed direction and offers more stability for older or lightweight machines. Some facing milling machines allow switching between the two. Slotting and Contour Facing Not every job is a square block. Face mills can be used for shallow slots or contoured faces if the toolpath is planned right. Just don’t expect perfect results unless your setup is rock solid. Face Milling Operations Summary Operation Type Description When to Use Conventional Face Milling Full-width surface passes General surface flattening Partial Face Milling Only part of cutter contacts surface Smaller or irregular workpieces Climb Milling Cutter feeds with the work Best for finish (requires stable setup) Conventional Milling Cutter moves against feed Safer on older or flexible machines Slotting / Contour Facing Shallow pockets or curved surfaces Non-flat geometries, careful setups Best Practices for Cleaner Face Milling ( reddit ) You can have the best tools on the shelf, but if you don’t dial in your technique, the finish will show it. Here’s what separates clean cuts from chewed-up messes. ● Keep your toolpath smooth—avoid sharp corners or direction changes mid-cut. ● Use coolant when possible. It extends insert life and keeps chips out of the way. ● Watch your depth of cut—too deep and you’ll get chatter, too shallow and the tool may rub instead of cut. ● Rigid setup matters more than fancy tooling. If your part moves, your surface finish suffers. And finally, picking the right tool geometry matters. The insert’s shape, rake, and edge prep can make or break your finish, especially on tricky materials. Tool Geometry Cheat Sheet: Choosing the Right Insert Material Recommended Geometry Rake Angle Notes Mild Steel Positive rake, round tip +10° to +20° Reduces cutting force, good surface finish Aluminum Sharp edge, polished +20° or more Prevents built-up edge, clean finish Stainless Steel Honed edge, tough grade 0° to +10° Needs stronger insert, avoid sharp corners Cast Iron Negative rake, strong edge 0° or negative Stable cut, handles interrupted surfaces Titanium Positive rake, low feed +10° Reduce heat, avoid rubbing Choosing the wrong insert isn't just a waste of money, it'll eat your surface finish alive Master the Cut Before You Hit Cycle Start Face milling is one of those processes that rewards the prepared. The right face mill tool , a solid setup, and a bit of know-how can take your surface finish from “rough passable” to production-ready. And if you’d rather not deal with tool geometry, chip clearance, or babysitting a facing milling machine , we’ve got your back. JLCCNC handles everything from single prototypes to high-volume runs, so you can skip the trial-and-error and get perfect surfaces from day one. Not sure if CNC milling is even the right choice for your part? Check out our comparison of CNC machining vs sheet metal fabrication to make the right call before you commit. How the Face Milling Process Works Common Face Milling Tools Types of Face Milling Operations Best Practices for Cleaner Face Milling Master the Cut Before You Hit Cycle Start Face milling doesn’t get the spotlight much, but it’s one of those workhorse processes that keeps machining shops running smooth. If you’ve ever needed a flat surface that’s actually flat , you’ve relied on it, whether you realized it or not. So what exactly is face milling? Think of it as the process behind every perfectly squared metal block, every smooth aluminum plate, every clean surface that just feels right. It’s precise, fast, and oddly satisfying to watch. But it’s not just about spinning a tool across some metal. The cutter design, tool path, speeds, and setup all play a role in getting that crisp finish without wrecking your inserts or your workpiece. In this guide, we’re breaking down how face milling works, what tools you’ll need, the types of operations involved, and a few tips that’ll save your cutters, and your sanity. What Is Face Milling? (istock) Face milling is one of the most common, and most essential, processes in the machining world. It’s all about cutting a flat surface perpendicular to the tool’s axis, usually with a wide face mill cutter that skims across the top of the material. The result? A smooth, level finish that’s ready for the next operation. Unlike side milling , which cuts along the edge or profile of a part, face milling focuses on creating a clean, wide face. It’s often the first step in squaring up a workpiece or prepping raw stock in a facing milling machine . What makes it effective is the tool design. A face mill tool typically uses multiple cutting edges (inserts) mounted in a circular holder. These inserts do most of the work, shaving off material in fast, controlled passes. You’ll find face mills in CNC shops, manual mills, and production floors alike, especially where consistency and finish quality matter. How the Face Milling Process Works The concept is simple: a rotating face mill sweeps across the surface of your material, cutting with the edges on the bottom of the tool. The setup, however, is where the real work begins. In a typical operation, the facing mill is mounted in a vertical spindle. As it spins, the inserts take shallow bites out of the material with each pass. The machine feeds the workpiece horizontally while the tool keeps cutting, layer by layer. It’s fast, consistent, and perfect for prepping a surface for tight-tolerance parts. The results depend on your setup, feed rate, cutting speed, tool path, and depth of cut all play a role. A roughing pass might take off more material quickly, while a finishing pass uses a finer face milling cutter for that clean, reflective finish. Tool rigidity and part stability matter. If your setup flexes, the finish suffers. If your inserts are dull, you’ll get chatter and uneven cuts. It's the kind of job where details make all the difference, and a decent face milling machine won't cover for poor planning. Roughing vs Finishing Parameter Roughing Finishing Depth of Cut 2–5 mm (0.08–0.2 in) 0.2–1 mm (0.01–0.04 in) Feed Rate Higher (aggressive) Lower (controlled) Cutting Speed Moderate Higher Tool Used Indexable face mill Fly cutter / fine-tooth mill Surface Finish Coarse Smooth (low Ra value) Common Face Milling Tools There’s more than one way to flatten a surface, and the tool you pick makes a big difference on your finish, your cycle time, and your tooling cost. Let’s break down the most common options used in face milling . Tool Selection Guide: When to Use What Tool Type Best For Pros Cons Face Mill Cutter General purpose, roughing + finishing Fast, efficient, easy insert swap Higher upfront cost Shell Mill Large parts, modular setups Versatile, scalable Needs arbor and holder setup Fly Cutter Finishing small to medium surfaces Inexpensive, smooth finish Slow, can vibrate at high speeds Solid Carbide Tool Light machines, tight spaces Rigid, compact Pricey, limited insert options Types of Face Milling Operations (ResearchGate) Face milling isn’t just about plowing a tool across a block of metal. There are different ways to run the cut, and knowing the options helps you get better results, or avoid screwing things up. Conventional Face Milling This is your go-to method. The face mill cuts across the entire top of the workpiece, removing material in overlapping passes. It’s efficient and ideal for prepping flat surfaces quickly. Partial Face Milling When the workpiece is smaller or has tricky geometry, only part of the face milling cutter engages with the material. It requires a bit more care in setup to avoid deflection and uneven cuts. Climb vs. Conventional Milling In climb milling, the cutter moves in the same direction as the feed, great finish, but it needs a solid machine. Conventional milling moves against the feed direction and offers more stability for older or lightweight machines. Some facing milling machines allow switching between the two. Slotting and Contour Facing Not every job is a square block. Face mills can be used for shallow slots or contoured faces if the toolpath is planned right. Just don’t expect perfect results unless your setup is rock solid. Face Milling Operations Summary Operation Type Description When to Use Conventional Face Milling Full-width surface passes General surface flattening Partial Face Milling Only part of cutter contacts surface Smaller or irregular workpieces Climb Milling Cutter feeds with the work Best for finish (requires stable setup) Conventional Milling Cutter moves against feed Safer on older or flexible machines Slotting / Contour Facing Shallow pockets or curved surfaces Non-flat geometries, careful setups Best Practices for Cleaner Face Milling ( reddit ) You can have the best tools on the shelf, but if you don’t dial in your technique, the finish will show it. Here’s what separates clean cuts from chewed-up messes. ● Keep your toolpath smooth—avoid sharp corners or direction changes mid-cut. ● Use coolant when possible. It extends insert life and keeps chips out of the way. ● Watch your depth of cut—too deep and you’ll get chatter, too shallow and the tool may rub instead of cut. ● Rigid setup matters more than fancy tooling. If your part moves, your surface finish suffers. And finally, picking the right tool geometry matters. The insert’s shape, rake, and edge prep can make or break your finish, especially on tricky materials. Tool Geometry Cheat Sheet: Choosing the Right Insert Material Recommended Geometry Rake Angle Notes Mild Steel Positive rake, round tip +10° to +20° Reduces cutting force, good surface finish Aluminum Sharp edge, polished +20° or more Prevents built-up edge, clean finish Stainless Steel Honed edge, tough grade 0° to +10° Needs stronger insert, avoid sharp corners Cast Iron Negative rake, strong edge 0° or negative Stable cut, handles interrupted surfaces Titanium Positive rake, low feed +10° Reduce heat, avoid rubbing Choosing the wrong insert isn't just a waste of money, it'll eat your surface finish alive Master the Cut Before You Hit Cycle Start Face milling is one of those processes that rewards the prepared. The right face mill tool , a solid setup, and a bit of know-how can take your surface finish from “rough passable” to production-ready. Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals High-Speed CNC Machining: What It Is and When to Use It Published Jul 04, 2025, updated Jul 30, 2026 6 min Table of Contents What Is High-Speed CNC Machining, Really? What Makes High-Speed Machining Possible? When to Use High-Speed CNC Machining When NOT to Use High-Speed Machining HSC vs. Traditional CNC: A Summary Industry Examples of HSC in Action Conclusion: Speed Is a Tool, Not a Shortcut In the world of precision manufacturing, speed isn't just about working faster—it's about working smarter. High-speed CNC machining (HSC) is often misunderstood as simply “spinning the spindle faster,” but in practice, it's a sophisticated, multi-variable strategy that blends tooling, motion control, thermal dynamics, and material science. For engineers, machinists, and manufacturers dealing with complex geometries, tight tolerances, and short lead times, high-speed machining isn’t a trend—it’s a competitive advantage. This article explores what HSC really is, how it differs from traditional methods, when it's worth using, and when it's not. (pexels) What Is High-Speed CNC Machining, Really? There’s no universal speed threshold that defines HSC, but in practical terms, it refers to machining processes that operate at: High spindle speeds : typically 15,000 to 60,000 RPM High feed rates : over 10 m/min, sometimes exceeding 30 m/min Low depth-of-cut with high material removal rates Optimized tool paths : using adaptive or trochoidal milling strategies Minimized cutting forces : preserving tool and machine integrity But the speed itself isn’t the defining factor— it’s the system’s ability to maintain stability and accuracy at those speeds . It’s Not Just Faster. It’s Fundamentally Different. Where traditional CNC milling relies on deeper, heavier cuts at lower speeds and forces, high-speed machining uses lighter, faster passes —reducing heat buildup, tool deflection, and mechanical stress. This results in smoother finishes, tighter tolerances, and in many cases, a shorter overall cycle time despite the “lighter” passes. What Makes High-Speed Machining Possible? To achieve HSC, you need more than just a high-RPM spindle. The entire machine system—hardware, software, tooling, and fixturing—needs to be designed or upgraded for high-speed operation: 1. Machine Tool Construction Stiff yet lightweight structures : minimize vibration and thermal distortion High-acceleration linear guides and ball screws : for rapid tool positioning Advanced control systems : with look-ahead features, dynamic path optimization, and jerk control 2. Spindle Technology High-speed spindles with minimal runout : critical for maintaining balance at high RPMs Oil-air or hybrid ceramic bearings : to handle thermal loads Integrated cooling : to stabilize performance over long runs 3. Tooling & Workholding Balanced, high-flute-count end mills : optimized for chip evacuation and lower force Heat-resistant coatings : like DLC or TiAlN for longevity Precision holders : such as shrink-fit or hydraulic chucks for minimal runout 4. CAM and Toolpath Strategy High-speed machining shines when paired with intelligent toolpaths such as: Adaptive clearing Trochoidal milling Constant engagement strategies These help maintain consistent cutting forces and prevent sudden tool load spikes. When to Use High-Speed CNC Machining 1. Thin-Walled or Delicate Parts Lightweight aerospace brackets and even medical housings often require minimal vibration and tight tolerances. HSC enables: Reduced tool deflection Low cutting forces that prevent wall distortion Minimal finishing post-processes 2. Hard Materials or Hardened Tool Steels For mold & die applications or cutting materials like Inconel, hardened steel, or titanium, high-speed machining with optimized tooling can: Prevent work hardening Improve surface finish Eliminate secondary operations (like EDM or polishing) 3. Aluminum and Non-Ferrous Materials Materials like 6061 and 7075 aluminum alloys respond exceptionally well to HSC, especially in high-volume applications like consumer electronics or automotive parts. You get: Mirror-like finishes High throughput Reduced burr formation 4. Complex 3D Geometries When working with sculpted surfaces—such as impellers, orthopedic implants, or molds—HSC, especially with 5-axis setups, can: Handle fine details Reduce machining time on intricate forms Improve surface quality, especially with ball-end tools 5. Prototyping and Short Lead Time Jobs High-speed setups often allow faster first part delivery , even if the roughing cycle is slightly longer. Combined with modern CAM software, you can go from CAD to chip in record time. When NOT to Use High-Speed Machining Despite its advantages, HSC isn’t always the right tool for the job. It’s best to avoid HSC when: 1. Roughing Large Steel Blocks Traditional low-RPM roughing with indexable tooling is more efficient for removing hundreds of cubic centimeters of material quickly. 2. Your Machine Can’t Handle It If your CNC has low spindle RPMs, insufficient rigidity, or outdated motion control, forcing HSC strategies can lead to: Tool chatter Premature wear Inconsistent finishes or even spindle damage 3. Cost Is a Bigger Concern Than Quality If you’re making simple brackets with loose tolerances in high quantities, the return on HSC investment may not be justified. HSC vs. Traditional CNC: A Summary Feature High-Speed CNC Traditional CNC Cutting Strategy Many light, fast passes Few heavy, slower passes Best Use Cases Precision, complex parts Bulk material removal Surface Finish Excellent Good to Fair Tool Life (with setup) Longer Shorter (under heavy load) Machine Requirements High-rigidity, advanced control Standard Learning Curve Steeper (toolpaths, setup) Moderate Cycle Time Often faster for complex parts Faster for simple roughing Industry Examples of HSC in Action ✦ Aerospace: Machining 7075 aluminum wing ribs with HSC can reduce cycle time by 30–40% and improve fatigue performance thanks to smoother edges and fewer stress concentrators. ✦ Medical: Hip implants and dental components require both biocompatible materials and flawless surface finishes—ideal for 5-axis high-speed strategies using ceramic-coated tools. ✦ Mold & Die: Direct machining of hardened tool steel with ball-nose end mills using HSC avoids lengthy EDM processes, accelerating time-to-market for injection molds. Conclusion: Speed Is a Tool, Not a Shortcut High-speed CNC machining is more than just running fast—it’s about optimizing every component in the machining system to cut more efficiently, more accurately, and with better repeatability . For engineers and manufacturing professionals, understanding when to adopt HSC—and when not to—is critical . Used properly, it’s a tool that can dramatically enhance part quality, lead time, and profitability. Misused, it’s a shortcut to broken tools and burnt-out spindles. If your work involves precision surfaces, tight tolerances, or high-mix low-volume production, HSC might be the secret weapon your process has been missing. What Is Laser Marking? Aluminum6061 laser marking Laser marking is a non-contact process that uses a focused laser beam to create visible or machine-readable identification directly on a manufactured part. The beam changes the surface condition rather than adding an external label or ink layer. Depending on the substrate and process settings, the mark may result from a surface-color change, oxidation, a change in texture, or localized coating or material removal. Common applications include serial numbers, part and revision codes, Data Matrix codes, and logos used for identification and traceability. The word "mark" covers several different surface changes. Which one you get depends on the material, the laser and the settings. Surface change What happens at the surface Where it typically shows up Oxidation (annealing) Heat forms a thin oxide layer that darkens or colors the surface Stainless steel, titanium Coating removal (ablation) The beam vaporizes a thin coating to expose the base metal Anodized aluminum, coated or painted metal Micro-recess or melted texture The surface melts or vaporizes slightly, changing roughness and reflectivity Bare metals Carbonization Heat chars or chemically darkens the surface Plastics, organic materials These surface-change mechanisms explain how laser marking can work across different substrates. They do not represent the complete list of materials or marking methods available for every JLCCNC order. Confirm material compatibility and the required appearance for the specific part. Precision CNC Machining Service Professional manufacturing, fast turnaround, and quality assurance. Get Instant Quote How Does the Laser Marking Process Work? Fiber laser marking system Preparing the Part and Marking File The marking artwork is loaded into the laser software in a supported format, with the part's marking face and position defined on the 2D drawing. The workpiece is positioned to maintain the required marking location and focus. Process settings are selected for the material and required surface effect, and a preliminary mark can be used to check contrast and detail before production. For new material and finish combinations, a sample mark can be used to confirm contrast and detail before production. Shops commonly run a test mark on a spare or scrap piece first. How the Laser Forms the Mark The laser system and its process settings must be suitable for the material and the required marking effect. In systems that use galvanometer scanning, mirrors steer the focused beam along the programmed path in the marking file. The focused beam concentrates energy in a localized area of the workpiece. Depending on the material and process settings, the interaction can change the surface color, modify the texture, remove a compatible coating, or remove substrate material to form a recess. The resulting mark depends on the interaction between the material, surface condition, and process settings. Verifying the Finished Mark Inspect the finished mark for edge definition, consistency of contrast, and conformity to the specified location. Check the marked area against the drawing requirements, including depth where specified. For machine-readable codes, verify readability using the intended scanner and inspection conditions. Verify machine-readable marks with the scanner and inspection setup used for the application. The laser etching guide linked above also recommends testing the code with the actual scanner you'll use in production. What Is the Difference Between Laser Marking, Laser Engraving, and Laser Etching? Term Typical surface change Material removal Result Laser marking Broad term for creating marks through laser-induced surface changes Depends on the method Visible identifiers, patterns, or codes Laser etching Usually creates contrast through a shallow surface modification Generally limited, depending on the process A visible mark with altered surface appearance Laser engraving Removes substrate material to create a recess Deliberate material removal A recessed mark that may be tactile These terms are not used consistently by every supplier, so the process name alone does not define the resulting feature. Specify the required appearance, recess depth where applicable, readability, and expected wear conditions. Suppliers do not always use these terms in the same way. In one quotation, "laser marking" may refer to a broad class of surface-modification processes; in another, it may describe a specific process. For reliable manufacturing results, define the required surface effect and measurable acceptance criteria instead of relying on terminology alone. Define the required appearance, recess depth where applicable, readability, and expected wear conditions. Specify whether the mark needs to contrast with the surrounding surface, whether a machine-readable code must pass a particular verification process, and whether later cleaning or surface treatments could affect the result. JLCCNC's design guide for laser marking specifies a recessed laser-marking depth of 0.03–0.1 mm. This is a JLCCNC-specific design specification, not a universal boundary between laser marking, etching, and engraving. Define the required appearance and depth on the drawing where applicable. Which Materials and Surface Finishes Can Be Laser Marked? How Material and Surface Finish Affect Marking Results The same artwork can produce different results depending on the material, surface finish and marking conditions. Reflectivity, roughness and existing coatings all affect contrast and final appearance. Material response and surface condition affect the resulting mark. Reflectivity, roughness, coatings, and the required surface effect all influence the process settings and the final contrast. Settings that work on one material or finish should not automatically be assumed to work on another. JLCCNC states that metal marking color is determined primarily by the characteristics of the material being marked, and its design guidance adds that results vary with surface roughness. A bead-blasted face and a smooth machined face won't look alike, even with identical settings. Surface treatments also affect the finished mark. Anodized aluminum and bare aluminum should not be assumed to produce the same contrast, even when the artwork is identical. Specify the actual surface finish and confirm the required appearance for that material before production. Materials Supported by JLCCNC JLCCNC offers laser marking for eligible CNC-machined and sheet metal parts. Material and finish availability depends on the selected manufacturing process and ordering requirements. Confirm the supported material, surface finish and marking requirements before production. Materials outside the confirmed laser-marking scope may require another identification method. UV printing is an alternative for compatible substrates when color is required, but material suitability should be confirmed before selecting the process. See JLCCNC's guide to laser marking vs. UV printing for a comparison of the two methods. Aluminum has its own behavior, especially anodized versus bare. Details live in our laser engraving aluminum article. Need laser marking for a custom part? Upload your CAD file for a project-specific quote. Define the marking surface and position on the 2D drawing, and provide the artwork in the required format. For sheet metal parts, follow the applicable file and ordering requirements. Precision CNC Machining Service Professional manufacturing, fast turnaround, and quality assurance. Get Instant Quote What Are the Benefits and Limitations of Laser Marking? Benefits of Laser Marking Technology Durability is a major advantage of laser marking. Because the mark is created by changing the surface rather than applying a separate adhesive label, it avoids label-edge peeling and ink-layer smearing. Long-term readability still depends on the marking method, material, surface finish, and service conditions. Laser marking does not require ink or adhesive label stock as part of the marking process, and the beam applies no stamping force to the workpiece. This avoids tool-to-part contact wear during marking, although the laser equipment and its optics still require appropriate maintenance. Laser marking can reproduce fine graphics and identification features without applying stamping force to the workpiece. Dot-peen marking creates physical indentations, while laser marking alters the surface through a laser-based process. The better option depends on the required appearance, readability, material, and operating environment. Machine-readable codes should be verified using the intended scanning setup. Laser marking is digitally controlled, so artwork can be revised without producing a new physical stamp or stencil. This can simplify mixed-batch production and product revisions, although actual cycle time depends on the graphic, the required surface effect, and the handling and verification steps involved. Limitations and Factors That Affect Marking Results These are the factors that decide whether a laser mark is the right call. Factor Why it matters What to specify Material and alloy Absorption and reflectivity change contrast Exact material and grade Surface finish and roughness Rough or uneven faces give inconsistent contrast Finish before marking Recess depth A shallow recess can wear through under heavy abrasion Wear and abrasion exposure Single-tone result Color follows the material, not the artwork Contrast expectations, not color names Geometry and access Curved or recessed faces change focus Which face, how flat Later finishing Blasting, plating or coating after marking can hurt legibility Mark after final finish where possible Any subsequent coating, blasting, heat treatment, or other finishing operation may alter the appearance or readability of a laser mark. Specify the complete process sequence and the required final appearance before production. If the part requires a pronounced tactile feature or must retain identification under severe abrasion, the appropriate marking method should be evaluated against those requirements rather than selected by name alone. What Are the Common Applications of Laser Marking? Part Identification and Traceability Laser marking supports part identification by placing a serial number, lot code, revision, or Data Matrix code directly on the component. When the identifier remains readable, production and inspection teams can link the physical part to its drawing revision, manufacturing records, and inspection results. Marking requirements vary by industry and application. Under U.S. FDA rules, a device that must bear a UDI on its label and is intended for repeated use and reprocessing generally must also carry a permanent direct marking, subject to applicable exceptions and alternatives. Automotive and aerospace manufacturers may also use serial numbers, part numbers, revision identifiers, or other traceability information according to their product and customer requirements. The marking method must be validated against the relevant requirements; laser marking alone does not establish regulatory compliance. On CNC-machined parts, the same practice applies at a smaller scale. A housing or bracket marked with its part number and revision allows incoming inspection to verify the part against the correct drawing revision. Logos, Labels, and Functional Markings Laser marking places a logo or product identifier directly on an enclosure or panel without requiring a separate adhesive label. Edge definition and contrast depend on the artwork, material, surface finish, and marking settings. The less obvious use is functional. Port and connector labels, orientation arrows, polarity marks, scale lines, calibration references, warning text on equipment panels. These aren't decoration. Incorrect or missing labels can create usability and safety issues on control panels. Laser-marked port labels, orientation arrows, polarity symbols, and warning text eliminate the need for a separate label, but readability should be checked against the expected cleaning and wear conditions. How Should CNC Parts Be Designed for Laser Marking? Define the marking face and positioning dimensions on the 2D drawing so the mark can be located without scaling an image. Supply the marking artwork in DWG or DXF at 1:1 scale, and clearly dimension the relevant geometry. JLCCNC recommends CAD-exported file formats and warns that machining precision cannot be guaranteed when other formats are used. For special shapes, provide the exact marking location and a dimension frame with clear instructions. Marking Location and Positioning Dimensions Identify the marking face and dimension its location from defined datum edges. Avoid relying on a scaled image to communicate position. JLCCNC's design guidance recommends a marking margin of usually 3 mm to help prevent incomplete patterns. For special geometries, show the exact marking location and the required dimensions on the drawing. Artwork, Character Size, and Code Readability Keep the artwork geometry clean, with lines thick enough to preserve the intended detail after marking. JLCCNC's design guide recommends a design-file resolution of at least 300 dpi for clear, detailed results. For DWG or DXF artwork, supply clean geometry at 1:1 scale; for bitmap elements, ensure the source image has sufficient resolution. The guide does not specify a universal minimum character height, line width, or Data Matrix size for laser marking. For machine-readable codes, define the required reading result and verify the mark using the intended scanner under the relevant inspection conditions. Mark Depth, Contrast, and Surface-Finish Requirements JLCCNC's design guide specifies a recessed laser-marking depth of 0.03–0.1 mm. Define the required marking appearance and depth where applicable, and identify any expected abrasion or cleaning exposure. If the marked area lies near a critical feature, include its location on the drawing so the effect on the part's functional requirements can be reviewed. Laser marking produces a single-tone result determined by the material and surface treatment rather than a freely selected artwork color. Define the required contrast against the actual finished surface, and confirm the expected appearance for the specified material and finish. Keep the mark off threads, sealing faces and tight-tolerance features. The recess is shallow, but it's still a local surface change. And if the part gets anodized or coated, mark after the final finish unless the process requires otherwise. Laser Marking FAQs Q: Is Laser Marking Permanent? Yes, for normal service. The beam changes the surface itself, so the mark won't peel, smear or fade like ink or a label. "Permanent" has limits though. A shallow recess can wear through under heavy, repeated abrasion, and marks on anodized parts depend on the coating staying put. If the part will be sanded, blasted or re-finished later, say so before marking. Q: Does Laser Marking Affect Part Dimensions or Surface Finish? Laser marking can alter the local surface. Some methods mainly change color or texture, while JLCCNC’s published laser-marking guidance specifies a recessed depth of 0.03–0.1 mm for our service. Keep marks away from critical sealing, threaded, mating, and tight-tolerance features, and show their location on the drawing. Q: What Recessed Depth Does JLCCNC's Laser Marking Service Produce? JLCCNC's laser marking produces a recessed depth of 0.03 to 0.1 mm. That sits between typical laser etching and typical laser engraving figures, which is why it helps to specify appearance and wear needs instead of relying on the process name. Q: Can Laser Marking Be Applied After CNC Machining? Yes, and that's the normal sequence. Machine the part, finish it, then mark it. At JLCCNC you select laser marking under Surface Finish when you order CNC parts, so machining and marking happen in one workflow. Marking after the final finish keeps the mark from being altered by later steps. Q: What Affects the Cost of Laser Marking CNC Parts? Several things, though the quote tool gives the real number. Material and finish set the settings needed. Mark size and complexity drive machine time. Quantity spreads setup across more parts. And drawing quality matters more than people think: missing positioning dimensions or non-CAD artwork cause delays, and delays cost money. Add laser marking in the instant quote to see pricing for your exact part.
