In systems that use galvanometer scanning, mirrors steer the focused beam along the programmed path in the marking file. The focused beam concentrates energy in a localized area of the workpiece. Depending on the material and process settings, the interaction can change the surface color, modify the texture, remove a compatible coating, or remove substrate material to form a recess. The resulting mark depends on the interaction between the material, surface condition, and process settings. Verifying the Finished Mark Inspect the finished mark for edge definition, consistency of contrast, and conformity to the specified location. Check the marked area against the drawing requirements, including depth where specified. For machine-readable codes, verify readability using the intended scanner and inspection conditions. Verify machine-readable marks with the scanner and inspection setup used for the application. The laser etching guide linked above also recommends testing the code with the actual scanner you'll use in production. What Is the Difference Between Laser Marking, Laser Engraving, and Laser Etching? Term Typical surface change Material removal Result Laser marking Broad term for creating marks through laser-induced surface changes Depends on the method Visible identifiers, patterns, or codes Laser etching Usually creates contrast through a shallow surface modification Generally limited, depending on the process A visible mark with altered surface appearance Laser engraving Removes substrate material to create a recess Deliberate material removal A recessed mark that may be tactile These terms are not used consistently by every supplier, so the process name alone does not define the resulting feature. Specify the required appearance, recess depth where applicable, readability, and expected wear conditions. Suppliers do not always use these terms in the same way. In one quotation, "laser marking" may refer to a broad class of surface-modification processes; in another, it may describe a specific process. For reliable manufacturing results, define the required surface effect and measurable acceptance criteria instead of relying on terminology alone. Define the required appearance, recess depth where applicable, readability, and expected wear conditions. Specify whether the mark needs to contrast with the surrounding surface, whether a machine-readable code must pass a particular verification process, and whether later cleaning or surface treatments could affect the result. JLCCNC's design guide for laser marking specifies a recessed laser-marking depth of 0.03–0.1 mm. This is a JLCCNC-specific design specification, not a universal boundary between laser marking, etching, and engraving. Define the required appearance and depth on the drawing where applicable. Which Materials and Surface Finishes Can Be Laser Marked? How Material and Surface Finish Affect Marking Results The same artwork can produce different results depending on the material, surface finish and marking conditions. Reflectivity, roughness and existing coatings all affect contrast and final appearance. Material response and surface condition affect the resulting mark. Reflectivity, roughness, coatings, and the required surface effect all influence the process settings and the final contrast. Settings that work on one material or finish should not automatically be assumed to work on another. JLCCNC states that metal marking color is determined primarily by the characteristics of the material being marked, and its design guidance adds that results vary with surface roughness. A bead-blasted face and a smooth machined face won't look alike, even with identical settings. Surface treatments also affect the finished mark. Anodized aluminum and bare aluminum should not be assumed to produce the same contrast, even when the artwork is identical. Specify the actual surface finish and confirm the required appearance for that material before production. Materials Supported by JLCCNC JLCCNC offers laser marking for eligible CNC-machined and sheet metal parts. Material and finish availability depends on the selected manufacturing process and ordering requirements. Confirm the supported material, surface finish and marking requirements before production. Materials outside the confirmed laser-marking scope may require another identification method. UV printing is an alternative for compatible substrates when color is required, but material suitability should be confirmed before selecting the process. See JLCCNC's guide to laser marking vs. UV printing for a comparison of the two methods. Aluminum has its own behavior, especially anodized versus bare. Details live in our laser engraving aluminum article. Need laser marking for a custom part? Upload your CAD file for a project-specific quote. Define the marking surface and position on the 2D drawing, and provide the artwork in the required format. For sheet metal parts, follow the applicable file and ordering requirements. Precision CNC Machining Service Professional manufacturing, fast turnaround, and quality assurance. Get Instant Quote What Are the Benefits and Limitations of Laser Marking? Benefits of Laser Marking Technology Durability is a major advantage of laser marking. Because the mark is created by changing the surface rather than applying a separate adhesive label, it avoids label-edge peeling and ink-layer smearing. Long-term readability still depends on the marking method, material, surface finish, and service conditions. Laser marking does not require ink or adhesive label stock as part of the marking process, and the beam applies no stamping force to the workpiece. This avoids tool-to-part contact wear during marking, although the laser equipment and its optics still require appropriate maintenance. Laser marking can reproduce fine graphics and identification features without applying stamping force to the workpiece. Dot-peen marking creates physical indentations, while laser marking alters the surface through a laser-based process. The better option depends on the required appearance, readability, material, and operating environment. Machine-readable codes should be verified using the intended scanning setup. Laser marking is digitally controlled, so artwork can be revised without producing a new physical stamp or stencil. This can simplify mixed-batch production and product revisions, although actual cycle time depends on the graphic, the required surface effect, and the handling and verification steps involved. Limitations and Factors That Affect Marking Results These are the factors that decide whether a laser mark is the right call. Factor Why it matters What to specify Material and alloy Absorption and reflectivity change contrast Exact material and grade Surface finish and roughness Rough or uneven faces give inconsistent contrast Finish before marking Recess depth A shallow recess can wear through under heavy abrasion Wear and abrasion exposure Single-tone result Color follows the material, not the artwork Contrast expectations, not color names Geometry and access Curved or recessed faces change focus Which face, how flat Later finishing Blasting, plating or coating after marking can hurt legibility Mark after final finish where possible Any subsequent coating, blasting, heat treatment, or other finishing operation may alter the appearance or readability of a laser mark. Specify the complete process sequence and the required final appearance before production. If the part requires a pronounced tactile feature or must retain identification under severe abrasion, the appropriate marking method should be evaluated against those requirements rather than selected by name alone. What Are the Common Applications of Laser Marking? Part Identification and Traceability Laser marking supports part identification by placing a serial number, lot code, revision, or Data Matrix code directly on the component. When the identifier remains readable, production and inspection teams can link the physical part to its drawing revision, manufacturing records, and inspection results. Marking requirements vary by industry and application. Under U.S. FDA rules, a device that must bear a UDI on its label and is intended for repeated use and reprocessing generally must also carry a permanent direct marking, subject to applicable exceptions and alternatives. Automotive and aerospace manufacturers may also use serial numbers, part numbers, revision identifiers, or other traceability information according to their product and customer requirements. The marking method must be validated against the relevant requirements; laser marking alone does not establish regulatory compliance. On CNC-machined parts, the same practice applies at a smaller scale. A housing or bracket marked with its part number and revision allows incoming inspection to verify the part against the correct drawing revision. Logos, Labels, and Functional Markings Laser marking places a logo or product identifier directly on an enclosure or panel without requiring a separate adhesive label. Edge definition and contrast depend on the artwork, material, surface finish, and marking settings. The less obvious use is functional. Port and connector labels, orientation arrows, polarity marks, scale lines, calibration references, warning text on equipment panels. These aren't decoration. Incorrect or missing labels can create usability and safety issues on control panels. Laser-marked port labels, orientation arrows, polarity symbols, and warning text eliminate the need for a separate label, but readability should be checked against the expected cleaning and wear conditions. How Should CNC Parts Be Designed for Laser Marking? Define the marking face and positioning dimensions on the 2D drawing so the mark can be located without scaling an image. Supply the marking artwork in DWG or DXF at 1:1 scale, and clearly dimension the relevant geometry. JLCCNC recommends CAD-exported file formats and warns that machining precision cannot be guaranteed when other formats are used. For special shapes, provide the exact marking location and a dimension frame with clear instructions. Marking Location and Positioning Dimensions Identify the marking face and dimension its location from defined datum edges. Avoid relying on a scaled image to communicate position. JLCCNC's design guidance recommends a marking margin of usually 3 mm to help prevent incomplete patterns. For special geometries, show the exact marking location and the required dimensions on the drawing. Artwork, Character Size, and Code Readability Keep the artwork geometry clean, with lines thick enough to preserve the intended detail after marking. JLCCNC's design guide recommends a design-file resolution of at least 300 dpi for clear, detailed results. For DWG or DXF artwork, supply clean geometry at 1:1 scale; for bitmap elements, ensure the source image has sufficient resolution. The guide does not specify a universal minimum character height, line width, or Data Matrix size for laser marking. For machine-readable codes, define the required reading result and verify the mark using the intended scanner under the relevant inspection conditions. Mark Depth, Contrast, and Surface-Finish Requirements JLCCNC's design guide specifies a recessed laser-marking depth of 0.03–0.1 mm. Define the required marking appearance and depth where applicable, and identify any expected abrasion or cleaning exposure. If the marked area lies near a critical feature, include its location on the drawing so the effect on the part's functional requirements can be reviewed. Laser marking produces a single-tone result determined by the material and surface treatment rather than a freely selected artwork color. Define the required contrast against the actual finished surface, and confirm the expected appearance for the specified material and finish. Keep the mark off threads, sealing faces and tight-tolerance features. The recess is shallow, but it's still a local surface change. And if the part gets anodized or coated, mark after the final finish unless the process requires otherwise. Laser Marking FAQs Q: Is Laser Marking Permanent? Yes, for normal service. The beam changes the surface itself, so the mark won't peel, smear or fade like ink or a label. "Permanent" has limits though. A shallow recess can wear through under heavy, repeated abrasion, and marks on anodized parts depend on the coating staying put. If the part will be sanded, blasted or re-finished later, say so before marking. Q: Does Laser Marking Affect Part Dimensions or Surface Finish? Laser marking can alter the local surface. Some methods mainly change color or texture, while JLCCNC’s published laser-marking guidance specifies a recessed depth of 0.03–0.1 mm for our service. Keep marks away from critical sealing, threaded, mating, and tight-tolerance features, and show their location on the drawing. Q: What Recessed Depth Does JLCCNC's Laser Marking Service Produce? JLCCNC's laser marking produces a recessed depth of 0.03 to 0.1 mm. That sits between typical laser etching and typical laser engraving figures, which is why it helps to specify appearance and wear needs instead of relying on the process name. Q: Can Laser Marking Be Applied After CNC Machining? Yes, and that's the normal sequence. Machine the part, finish it, then mark it. At JLCCNC you select laser marking under Surface Finish when you order CNC parts, so machining and marking happen in one workflow. Marking after the final finish keeps the mark from being altered by later steps. Q: What Affects the Cost of Laser Marking CNC Parts? Several things, though the quote tool gives the real number. Material and finish set the settings needed. Mark size and complexity drive machine time. Quantity spreads setup across more parts. And drawing quality matters more than people think: missing positioning dimensions or non-CAD artwork cause delays, and delays cost money. Add laser marking in the instant quote to see pricing for your exact part. Why Rake Angle is Critical in Machining Types of Rake Angle How to Get Rake Angle in a Cutting Tool Practical Tips for Choosing the Right Rake Angle Chip Control and Rake Angle FAQ Final Thoughts What is Rake Angle? (minaprem) If you've ever stood in front of a CNC machine or a manual lathe, you know that the cutting tool's geometry isn't just some arbitrary design. Every angle, edge, and surface has a job to do, and one of the most important of those is the rake angle . We've been running machines long enough to know that rake angle can make or break your surface finish, tool life, and machining efficiency. In this guide, we're going to walk you through what rake angle is, how it works, and how to choose the right one , without all the confusing textbook terms. The rake angle in a cutting tool is the angle between the tool\s rake face (the surface where the chip slides away) and a line perpendicular to the workpiece surface. Think of it as how much your tool “leans” into or away from the cut: Positive rake angle: The Tool face leans forward toward the cut Negative rake angle: The Tool face leans backward away from the cut Why it matters: rake angle affects chip formation, cutting forces, tool wear, and even surface finish. Why Rake Angle is Critical in Machining (Istock) In real-world machining, even a small change in cutting tool rake angle can: Lower or increase cutting forces Improve or worsen surface finish Extend or shorten tool life Affect chip control and heat dissipation A good rake angle means the tool slices material efficiently. A poor one? It plows through the workpiece, causing chatter, heat, and early tool failure. A well-chosen rake angle can dramatically improve your part's surface finish. For more practical tips, see our guide on How to Improve Surface Finish in CNC Machining . Types of Rake Angle 1. Positive Rake Angle (ResearchGate) Tool face leans toward the cut. Advantages: Lower cutting forces Smoother surface finish Less heat Disadvantages: Weaker cutting edge (prone to chipping) Best for: Aluminum, brass, plastics, and soft steels. 2. Negative Rake Angle (ResearchGate) The tool face leans away from the cut. Advantages: Stronger cutting edge Can handle hard materials and interrupted cuts Durable at high speeds and temps Disadvantages: Higher cutting forces More heat generation Best for: Titanium, hardened steels, nickel alloys, anywhere tool strength is priority. 3. Zero Rake Angle (Minaprem) Neutral cutting edge, neither forward nor backward lean. Best for: General turning, moderate toughness, balanced performance. How to Get Rake Angle in a Cutting Tool There are two main ways we get rake angle: 1. Built into the Tool Geometry Carbide inserts, HSS tools, or form tools come with a pre-designed rake angle. You choose the right insert geometry for the job. 2. By Tool Setup or Holder Design Sometimes, the toolholder itself provides a rake (especially in turning tools or milling cutters). Tilting the tool in the machine can also alter the effective rake angle. If you're wondering "how to get rake angle" , the answer is really about choosing the right insert grade and holder combo for your material, and making sure your setup matches your machining goals. Practical Tips for Choosing the Right Rake Angle For soft materials: Go positive. You'll thank yourself for the smoother cuts and smaller forces. For hard or abrasive materials: Go negative. Your edge will last longer. For interrupted cuts (like milling a part with keyways or turning across drilled holes): negative rake is usually safer. Always match feed rate & spindle speed to your rake angle, a positive rake can chatter if you feed too slowly. Chip Control and Rake Angle (FK instrument) One thing many beginners miss is how rake angle affects chip shape: Positive rake: Thinner, more curled chips Negative rake: Thicker, more segmented chips If you're trying to get those perfect “6” or “9”-shaped chips for safety and chip evacuation, adjusting rake angle is one of your most powerful tools. Need help picking the right cutting tool rake angle for your material? Upload your CAD file here , and we'll help you choose the perfect tooling setup for maximum efficiency. FAQ 1. What is rake angle in a cutting tool? The rake angle is the angle between the cutting tool's rake face (where the chip flows) and a line perpendicular to the workpiece surface. It controls how the tool enters the material, affects chip formation, cutting forces, and surface finish. 2. Why is rake angle important in machining? Rake angle directly impacts cutting efficiency, heat generation, and tool life. The right rake angle improves chip flow, reduces cutting forces, and helps you get a smoother finish. The wrong rake angle can cause tool wear, chatter, and poor part quality. 3. What is a negative rake angle and when should I use it? A negative rake angle means the cutting face leans away from the cut. It's best for hard, abrasive, or high-strength materials where tool edge durability matters more than ease of cutting. 4. What's the difference between positive and negative rake angles? Positive rake → Easier cutting, smoother finish, less heat, but weaker edge. Negative rake → Stronger edge, handles tough materials, but generates more cutting forces and heat. 5. How do you get the correct rake angle in machining? You can achieve a rake angle through the cutting tool's built-in geometry or by adjusting toolholder setup. Many CNC insert manufacturers specify the rake angle in their catalogs, so match it to your material and job type. 6. Does rake angle affect chip control? Yes! Positive rake angles create thin, curled chips, while negative rake angles produce thicker, more segmented chips. Adjusting rake angle can help prevent chip jamming and improve safety. 7. Can rake angle improve surface finish? Absolutely. A properly chosen rake angle slices the material instead of plowing it, resulting in a smoother, more accurate surface finish, especially on soft materials. Final Thoughts Rake angle isn't just a textbook term, it's a real-world lever you can pull to make machining faster, cleaner, and more cost-effective. If you've never paid attention to your rake angle before, start experimenting. You'll quickly see why it's one of the most important elements in cutting tool rake angle design and rake angle in machining performance. For more practical tips, see our guide on How to Improve Surface Finish in CNC Machining . Types of Rake Angle 1. Positive Rake Angle (ResearchGate) Tool face leans toward the cut. Advantages: Lower cutting forces Smoother surface finish Less heat Disadvantages: Weaker cutting edge (prone to chipping) Best for: Aluminum, brass, plastics, and soft steels. 2. Negative Rake Angle (ResearchGate) The tool face leans away from the cut. Advantages: Stronger cutting edge Can handle hard materials and interrupted cuts Durable at high speeds and temps Disadvantages: Higher cutting forces More heat generation Best for: Titanium, hardened steels, nickel alloys, anywhere tool strength is priority. 3. Zero Rake Angle (Minaprem) Neutral cutting edge, neither forward nor backward lean. Best for: General turning, moderate toughness, balanced performance. How to Get Rake Angle in a Cutting Tool There are two main ways we get rake angle: 1. Built into the Tool Geometry Carbide inserts, HSS tools, or form tools come with a pre-designed rake angle. You choose the right insert geometry for the job. 2. By Tool Setup or Holder Design Sometimes, the toolholder itself provides a rake (especially in turning tools or milling cutters). Tilting the tool in the machine can also alter the effective rake angle. If you're wondering "how to get rake angle" , the answer is really about choosing the right insert grade and holder combo for your material, and making sure your setup matches your machining goals. Practical Tips for Choosing the Right Rake Angle For soft materials: Go positive. You'll thank yourself for the smoother cuts and smaller forces. For hard or abrasive materials: Go negative. Your edge will last longer. For interrupted cuts (like milling a part with keyways or turning across drilled holes): negative rake is usually safer. Always match feed rate & spindle speed to your rake angle, a positive rake can chatter if you feed too slowly. Chip Control and Rake Angle (FK instrument) One thing many beginners miss is how rake angle affects chip shape: Positive rake: Thinner, more curled chips Negative rake: Thicker, more segmented chips If you're trying to get those perfect “6” or “9”-shaped chips for safety and chip evacuation, adjusting rake angle is one of your most powerful tools. Need help picking the right cutting tool rake angle for your material? Upload your CAD file here , and we'll help you choose the perfect tooling setup for maximum efficiency. FAQ 1. What is rake angle in a cutting tool? The rake angle is the angle between the cutting tool's rake face (where the chip flows) and a line perpendicular to the workpiece surface. It controls how the tool enters the material, affects chip formation, cutting forces, and surface finish. 2. Why is rake angle important in machining? Rake angle directly impacts cutting efficiency, heat generation, and tool life. The right rake angle improves chip flow, reduces cutting forces, and helps you get a smoother finish. The wrong rake angle can cause tool wear, chatter, and poor part quality. 3. What is a negative rake angle and when should I use it? A negative rake angle means the cutting face leans away from the cut. It's best for hard, abrasive, or high-strength materials where tool edge durability matters more than ease of cutting. 4. What's the difference between positive and negative rake angles? Positive rake → Easier cutting, smoother finish, less heat, but weaker edge. Negative rake → Stronger edge, handles tough materials, but generates more cutting forces and heat. 5. How do you get the correct rake angle in machining? You can achieve a rake angle through the cutting tool's built-in geometry or by adjusting toolholder setup. Many CNC insert manufacturers specify the rake angle in their catalogs, so match it to your material and job type. 6. Does rake angle affect chip control? Yes! Positive rake angles create thin, curled chips, while negative rake angles produce thicker, more segmented chips. Adjusting rake angle can help prevent chip jamming and improve safety. 7. Can rake angle improve surface finish? Absolutely. A properly chosen rake angle slices the material instead of plowing it, resulting in a smoother, more accurate surface finish, especially on soft materials. If you've never paid attention to your rake angle before, start experimenting. You'll quickly see why it's one of the most important elements in cutting tool rake angle design and rake angle in machining performance. Published Jul 30, 2025, updated Jul 28, 2025 5 min Threading a hole sounds simple, until you’re deciding between thread milling and tapping . Both methods are staples in CNC machining and manual operations, but they serve different purposes, machines, and tolerances. Whether you're threading aluminum, stainless steel, or titanium, choosing the wrong method can mean broken tools, scrapped parts, or wasted hours. Let’s break down the real differences between thread milling vs tapping , when to use one over the other, and how to choose the right tool for your part. What is Tapping? Tapping is the traditional method of creating internal threads by driving a tap, a hardened cutting tool, into a pre-drilled hole. It’s fast, easy to set up, and widely used in manual and CNC operations. There are three common types of taps: ● Hand taps – used manually with a T-handle ● Spiral point taps – best for through holes ● Spiral flute taps – best for blind holes Taps are typically specific to one thread size and pitch, which makes them convenient but rigid in flexibility. What is Thread Milling? Thread milling , on the other hand, uses a rotating tool called a thread mill to cut threads with a helical interpolation motion. The tool enters the hole and follows a spiral path to form the thread, using a CNC program to control pitch and depth. There are three types of thread mills: ● Single-point thread mills – extremely flexible for custom threads ● Multi-form thread mills – cut the full profile in one pass ● Indexable thread mills – ideal for large threads or production runs Thread milling may require more programming and setup time, but it shines in areas tapping simply can't reach. Thread Milling vs Tapping: Head-to-Head Comparison Let’s stack up thread milling vs tapping in the areas that matter most: Feature Tapping Thread Milling Speed Faster for high-volume production Slower, especially for large threads Tool Flexibility One tap per size/thread One thread mill can cut many sizes Material Suitability Risk of tap breakage in tough metals Better for hard-to-machine materials Thread Quality High-quality but fixed geometry Adjustable depth and excellent finish Chip Control Poor in blind holes Better evacuation and cleaner threads Cost Cheaper per tool Higher initial tool cost, lower long-term Thread Milling and Tapping in Different Materials When working with softer materials like aluminum or mild steel, tapping is fast and rarely problematic. But when dealing with: ● Stainless steel ● Tool steel ● Superalloys …thread milling provides better tool life and reduces the risk of tool breakage. This makes it a smart choice for aerospace, medical, and high-precision industries. CNC Programming Differences Tapping usually relies on a simple cycle (G84 for right-hand, G74 for left-hand tapping). Easy to program, minimal variables. Thread milling , on the other hand, requires: ● Circular interpolation (G02/G03) ● Depth control ● Helix angle programming While this adds complexity, modern CAM software and CNCs make it increasingly easier. Tool Life and Cost Considerations Taps wear out quickly in hard materials and can break, especially in blind holes with poor chip evacuation. Thread mills , although more expensive upfront, last longer and are more forgiving, especially if you’re threading near the bottom of a hole. Plus, if a thread mill breaks, you typically don’t lose the entire part. Is Thread Milling Better Than Tapping? It depends on your application. Tapping wins when: ● You're working in high-volume production ● Thread size and material are standard ● Speed and cost-per-hole are critical Thread milling is better when: ● You're threading expensive or difficult materials like Inconel or titanium ● You need flexibility in thread sizes or depths ● You want to avoid breaking taps in blind holes ● You're using CNC machines capable of helical interpolation So, is thread milling better than tapping ? In terms of flexibility and safety, yes. But in terms of speed and simplicity, tapping still holds the crown for everyday work. At JLCCNC , we specialize in precise, reliable threaded parts, no matter the size, material, or threading method. Whether you need help programming a thread milling cycle or want bulk tapping production , we’re here to help. Upload your design file and get a free quote here , we’ll recommend the best process for your job. Final Word: Which One Should You Use? Use tapping when: ● You need speed and low cost ● You’re working on large batches with consistent threads ● You have limited CNC capabilities Use thread milling when: ● You're working with tough or expensive materials ● Flexibility, precision, and thread quality matter ● You're threading blind holes or varying thread diameters Pro tip: If you’re threading critical parts, test both methods. A single broken tap can cost more than investing in a thread mill. Want More? Threading precision matters. Check out our guide on CNC tolerances and machining accuracy for a deeper understanding of how to control fit, finish, and dimensional repeatability. Whether you're working with tough materials, tight tolerances, or just want expert advice on choosing between thread milling and tapping , our CNC machining services have you covered. Upload your design file and get a free quote, let’s bring your part to life with accuracy and confidence. It’s a common question in fabrication, and one that sparks plenty of debate on shop floors and online forums alike: Waterjet or laser cutting? How to cut sheet metal in a way that gives you the cleanest cut, the best value, or the fastest turnaround? Here’s the thing: it’s not always a clear-cut answer. Both waterjet and laser cutting are precision powerhouses in the world of sheet metal fabrication. They each come with their own strengths, quirks, and best-use scenarios. Some projects demand the crisp accuracy of a laser, others the cold, abrasive power of high-pressure water, and sometimes, it’s a combination of both that gets the job done right. In this blog, we’re diving into the differences between waterjet and laser cutting , from how each method works to what materials they handle best, the cost and speed implications, and which process makes the most sense for your next job. If you’ve ever been torn between these two cutting technologies, we’re here to break it down, no fluff, just facts. Let’s get into it. Similarities Between Waterjet and Laser Cutting Before we dive into the differences, let’s clear one thing up: waterjet and laser cutting aren’t rivals as much as they are different tools in the same precision toolkit. In many ways, they share common ground, especially when it comes to their roles in modern sheet metal fabrication. Here are some key similarities: CNC Precision : Both processes rely on CNC (Computer Numerical Control) systems, meaning they’re incredibly accurate and highly repeatable. Once a CAD file is uploaded, both machines will follow it to the exact detail, cut after cut. No Physical Tooling Contact : Unlike traditional machining, neither method uses a physical cutting tool that touches the material. That means no tool wear , fewer mechanical stresses on the material, and a cleaner overall process. Versatility in Design : Both are ideal for cutting complex 2D profiles from sheet metal. Sharp corners, intricate curves, and tight inner contours? No problem for either. High Tolerances : Depending on the setup, both can achieve tolerances within a few thousandths of an inch. That level of precision makes them suitable for everything from aerospace components to high-end consumer products. Industry-Wide Applications : You’ll find waterjet and laser cutting used across a wide range of industries, automotive, aerospace, industrial design, signage, architecture, prototyping , and beyond. If it involves metal and demands clean, accurate cuts, chances are one of these methods is in play. Both waterjet and laser cutting are digitally controlled and offer excellent precision, making them powerful sheet metal cutting tools . Want to explore how laser compares to another popular digital method? Here's a detailed guide on the difference between CNC cutting and laser cutting. In short, both waterjet and laser cutting offer clean cuts, reliable repeatability, and flexible design possibilities . But once you start factoring in material type, thickness, budget, and speed, the differences really start to show. Speaking of which, let’s line them up side by side in a comparison table next. Waterjet vs Laser Cutting: Key Differences Feature/Factor Waterjet Cutting Laser Cutting Cutting Method High-pressure water + abrasive Focused laser beam Heat-Affected Zone (HAZ) None Present Ideal Materials Metals, stone, glass, composites Metals, some plastics, thin woods Max Thickness (Sheet Metal) Up to 6+ inches Typically under 1 inch (varies by metal) Tolerance/Precision ~±0.003" to ±0.005" ~±0.001" to ±0.003" Kerf Width Wider (~0.02" - 0.04") Narrower (~0.006" - 0.012") Cutting Speed Slower, especially on thick material Faster on thin-to-medium materials Surface Finish Matte/sanded edge Clean, slightly discolored edge Secondary Processing Often needed Often minimal Cost Comparison: Which Sheet Metal Cutting Method Saves More? (source: Freepik) When it comes to sheet metal cutting , cost is often the deciding factor, especially for production runs or budget-sensitive projects. While both waterjet cutting and laser cutting of metal sheets offer precision and versatility, the overall expense of each method can vary widely depending on a few key factors. Let’s break it down: 1. Equipment and Operation Costs Laser cutting machines tend to have a higher upfront investment. However, they’re generally faster and more energy-efficient , which can reduce per-part costs over time, especially for thinner materials. Waterjet cutting systems , on the other hand, come with lower thermal risk but higher ongoing costs due to the use of abrasive materials , pumps, and higher maintenance needs. 2. Consumables and Power Use Laser cutters primarily use gas (like nitrogen or oxygen) and electricity. These costs scale with power and material thickness, but there’s no abrasive to replace. Waterjets consume a lot of water and require a constant supply of garnet abrasive. Over time, abrasive costs can add up significantly , especially for long or thick cuts. 3. Maintenance and Downtime Waterjet systems have more moving parts and higher wear-and-tear from the abrasive flow. Expect more downtime for maintenance and consumable replacement. Laser cutters require less mechanical upkeep, which means more uptime and faster production cycles , particularly for thin cut sheet metal jobs. 4. Material Waste and Post-Processing Laser cutting sheet metal usually produces cleaner edges with minimal kerf, which means less post-processing and lower finishing costs. Waterjet cutting might leave a rougher edge or more taper, especially on thick stock, which could require additional machining. 5. Real-World Cost Examples For thin-gauge materials like aluminum or stainless steel (under 1/4"), laser cutting is typically the most cost-effective way to cut sheet metal , faster, cleaner, and more economical per part. For thick or exotic materials (like titanium, stone, or composites), waterjet cutting may be more cost-effective despite slower speeds, since it doesn’t risk warping the material or requiring costly rework. Speed and Precision: Which Sheet Metal Cutting Tool Performs Better? (source: Pexels) In sheet metal fabrication, speed and precision aren’t just nice-to-haves, they’re make-or-break factors. Whether you’re cranking out hundreds of parts or creating a one-off prototype, the right sheet metal cutting tool can dramatically impact turnaround time and final quality. Let’s see how sheet meta l laser cutting and waterjet cutting stack up when it comes to cutting speed and edge precision. Speed: Laser Wins the Race (Most of the Time) Laser cutting is incredibly quick, particularly when working with thin to medium-thickness metal sheets. The focused laser beam can slice through materials like stainless steel or aluminum with incredible efficiency. If you're cutting a run of 0.125" stainless brackets, for example, laser cutting sheet metal might finish the entire job in minutes. Compare that to waterjet cutting, while it’s powerful, it’s not known for speed . The process is slower because it mechanically erodes the material rather than vaporizing it. A 0.5" thick aluminum plate might take a waterjet several minutes to cut through, whereas a laser would be done in a fraction of the time, assuming the thickness is within the laser's optimal range. Example: Cutting a batch of 1/8" mild steel electrical enclosures? Go with laser cutting for quicker production. Cutting a custom piece from 2" thick steel? Waterjet’s your best bet. Precision: Depends on the Material and Thickness Both methods are highly accurate , but they shine under different conditions. Laser cutting delivers ultra-fine detail and tighter tolerances, often as precise as ±0.001", especially on thinner materials. This makes it ideal for projects requiring tight fitment, intricate geometries , or minimal post-processing. Waterjet cutting is also accurate, generally around ±0.003" to ±0.005", but it can suffer from tapering on thick materials if not properly controlled. However, it has a great advantage: no heat-affected zone (HAZ) . That means zero risk of material warping, which can preserve mechanical properties in heat-sensitive metals. Example: Need finely detailed stainless steel signage with sharp internal cutouts? Laser cutting is the answer. Cutting heat-treated tool steel or titanium that can’t afford any heat distortion? Waterjet wins. Edge Quality: Smooth vs. Matte Laser cutting leaves a smooth, often shiny edge, great for visible parts or components going straight to assembly. Waterjet typically leaves a matte, sandblasted edge. It's clean, but may require extra finishing if aesthetics matter. Materials & Thickness: What Can You Cut (and How Thick)? (source: Unsplash) When it comes to how to cut sheet metal , your material choice and thickness often make the decision for you. Laser cutting excels with thin to moderately thick metal sheets<dynamic-value> aluminum, stainless, and mild steel up to around 0.75". It struggles with highly reflective materials (like copper) and anything too thick, which can reduce cut quality or slow production significantly. Waterjet cutting , on the other hand, can slice through virtually anything: metals, composites, stone, even glass , and up to 6 inches thick or more . No melting, no HAZ, and no material limitations. Quick takeaway: If you're working with thick or exotic materials, waterjet is your go-to. For fast, clean cuts on standard gauge metal, laser cutting is typically more efficient. What is CNC Technology? CNC technology refers to the integrated use of software, control systems, and automated machinery to manage and execute precision manufacturing processes. In modern production environments, CNC technology functions as a core manufacturing platform—linking digital design data with machining operations, tool management, and quality control systems. Advantages of CNC Technology CNC technology offers a wide range of advantages that make it essential to modern manufacturing. By combining computer-controlled automation with high-performance machinery, CNC systems significantly improve manufacturing efficiency. They also enable superior quality and scalability across diverse industries. High Precision and Consistent Accuracy One of the most significant advantages of CNC technology is its ability to deliver extremely high precision. CNC technology can repeatedly produce components with tight tolerances that are difficult or impossible to achieve through manual machining. Once a program is validated, the same dimensions and surface quality can be maintained across thousands of parts, ensuring consistent accuracy even in complex geometries. This level of precision is especially critical in industries such as aerospace, automotive, medical devices, and electronics, where small dimensional deviations can affect performance, safety, or compliance with industry standards. Increased Production Efficiency CNC technology dramatically improves production efficiency by automating machining operations. Machines can run continuously with minimal operator intervention, reducing setup time and accelerating production cycles. Multi-axis CNC systems further enhance efficiency by completing multiple operations—such as milling, drilling, and contouring—in a single setup. Automated tool changes, optimized tool paths, and high-speed machining capabilities allow manufacturers to shorten lead times and respond quickly to changing production demands. Excellent Repeatability and Quality Control Repeatability is a core strength of CNC technology. Every part produced from the same CNC program is virtually identical, minimizing variation and reducing scrap rates. This repeatability simplifies quality control processes, as fewer manual inspections are required once a process is stabilized. CNC systems also integrate easily with in-process measurement and inspection technologies, enabling real-time quality monitoring and early detection of deviations before defects occur. Material and Design Versatility CNC technology supports a wide range of materials, including metals, plastics, composites, and engineered alloys. From aluminum and stainless steel to advanced polymers and titanium, CNC machines can be optimized to handle different cutting characteristics and surface finish requirements. A common example is aluminum CNC machining , which is widely used due to aluminum’s excellent machinability and strength-to-weight ratio. In addition, CNC technology enables the machining of complex shapes, internal features, and intricate contours that would be extremely time-consuming or impractical with conventional methods. This design freedom allows engineers to innovate without being limited by manufacturing constraints. Scalability from Prototyping to Mass Production Another key advantage of CNC technology is its scalability. The same CNC setup can be used for rapid prototyping, small-batch production, and high-volume manufacturing with minimal modification. Design changes can be implemented quickly by updating the digital program rather than retooling entire production lines. This flexibility is particularly valuable for startups, R&D teams, and manufacturers operating in fast-moving markets where product iterations are frequent. Reduced Labor Dependency and Improved Safety By automating machining tasks, CNC technology reduces reliance on manual labor and lowers the risk of human error. Operators are less exposed to cutting tools and moving machine components, resulting in a safer working environment. Modern CNC systems also feature built-in safety controls, error detection, and machine monitoring functions that further protect both personnel and equipment while maintaining stable production. Cost Efficiency Over the Product Lifecycle While CNC machines require an initial investment, they offer long-term cost advantages. Reduced material waste, lower rework rates, shorter production times, and improved machine utilization all contribute to a lower cost per part over the product lifecycle. For manufacturers seeking consistent quality, predictable output, and efficient resource usage, CNC technology represents a cost-effective solution that supports sustainable growth. Applications of CNC Technology in Manufacturing CNC technology has a wide range of applications across industries due to its ability to deliver high precision, consistency, and production efficiency. From large-scale industrial manufacturing to rapid prototyping, CNC technology continues to expand as materials, software, and machine capabilities evolve. Applications in Metalworking CNC milling machines, lathes, and laser cutters handle metals like aluminum, steel, and titanium with unmatched precision. These machines reduce manual labor, minimize errors, and allow for complex shapes that meet rigorous industry standards. In metalworking industries where tolerance control and material consistency are critical, CNC technology enables reliable production of complex metal components at scale. Applications in Plastics and Woodworking Beyond metals, CNC routers can cut, engrave, and shape plastic components or wood panels with high accuracy. Routers are typically used for wood and plastic materials, while milling machines are better suited for metal machining due to their rigidity and cutting capabilities. Manufacturers can efficiently produce prototypes and mass-produced items, lowering production costs and turnaround times. Industrial Applications Industries such as automotive, aerospace, electronics, energy, and heavy machinery rely on CNC systems to produce structural components, housings, brackets, and precision parts. CNC machining ensures tight tolerances, repeatability, and high reliability for critical components. Prototyping and Small Batch Production Rapid prototyping and small-batch CNC production allow engineers to quickly transform digital designs into functional prototypes, enabling faster design validation, iterative testing, and reduced time-to-market. Innovative Uses in Various Industries Advanced applications such as multi-axis cutting, hybrid additive-subtractive manufacturing, and complex 3D contour machining expand possibilities in medical devices, architecture, and custom design. CNC Machine Technology Types of CNC Machines CNC machine technology includes milling machines, lathes, routers, plasma cutters, and laser engraving systems. Each type serves a specific function, from cutting and drilling to shaping and engraving, meeting diverse manufacturing needs. How CNC Machines Work CNC machines operate by translating digital designs into precise machining actions through integrated control systems. This enables highly accurate and repeatable production while minimizing material waste and optimizing workflow efficiency. Maintenance and Optimization Proper maintenance of CNC machines is essential for long-term performance. Regular calibration, tool replacement, and software updates optimize machine efficiency and prevent downtime. Skilled operators can further enhance productivity by choosing the right tooling and machining parameters. Industrial CNC Technology Automation in Large-Scale Production Industrial CNC technology enables full automation of production lines. Large-scale manufacturing can run continuously with minimal human supervision, improving throughput and reducing labor costs. Integration with Industrial Processes CNC technology integrates seamlessly with industrial processes such as assembly, quality inspection, and material handling. This integration allows for smarter factories, streamlined workflows, and higher overall efficiency. Case Studies Industries adopting industrial CNC technology have reported reduced production errors, faster turnaround times, and improved product consistency. For example, automotive suppliers use CNC machines to produce engine components with precise tolerances, enhancing vehicle performance and reliability. CNC Technology Services Design and Consulting Services CNC technology services extend beyond machining itself. Design and consulting services help manufacturers apply CNC technology effectively by optimizing material selection, machining strategies, and process planning before production begins. Manufacturing and Prototyping Services Service providers offer CNC machining for both prototypes and mass production. This allows businesses to outsource specialized tasks, reduce overhead, and maintain high-quality standards. Maintenance and Support Services Many CNC technology service providers also offer ongoing maintenance, troubleshooting, and training. This ensures clients can maintain efficient operations, extend machine lifespan, and minimize production delays. Future Trends in CNC Technology Beyond basic CNC operation and machine control, future CNC technology development is increasingly driven by intelligence, connectivity, and system-level integration. Future developments will not only improve precision and productivity but also fundamentally reshape how factories operate, how products are designed, and how manufacturers compete in global markets. Smart CNC and AI Integration The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with CNC systems is transforming machining from reactive automation into predictive and adaptive manufacturing. AI-powered algorithms can analyze historical machining data. They automatically optimize tool paths, reduce cycle times, and minimize tool wear. Machine learning models are increasingly used to detect subtle signs of tool degradation or misalignment before they cause defects. In aerospace and medical device manufacturing, where tolerances are extremely tight, AI-assisted CNC tool path optimization is already being adopted to ensure consistency and precision across complex geometries. Over time, smart CNC machines will be able to adjust cutting strategies in real time, self-correcting for material inconsistencies and dynamic load variations without human intervention. IoT and Connected Manufacturing The rise of the Internet of Things (IoT) enables CNC machines to become integral components of connected smart factories. Sensors embedded in CNC equipment collect real-time data on temperature, vibration, spindle load, and tool life. This data, streamed through secure networks, feeds into centralized manufacturing execution systems (MES) and enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems to support real-time monitoring and informed decision-making. Connected CNC machines can automatically schedule maintenance based on actual usage patterns, reducing unplanned downtime. In facilities with multiple machines producing different parts, IoT connectivity enhances workflow coordination, material tracking, and quality control, leading to higher operational efficiency and lower production costs. Advanced Materials and Machining Techniques As new materials continue to emerge, CNC technology evolves to address the challenges they present. Advanced composites, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) , and next-generation polymers have unique machining requirements. High-entropy alloys are composed of multiple principal elements in near-equal proportions, offering exceptional strength, wear resistance, and thermal stability. These materials are increasingly used in aerospace and energy applications, where CNC machining must precisely control cutting forces and heat generation to maintain part integrity. CNC technology is also incorporating hybrid manufacturing techniques that combine additive manufacturing (3D printing) with traditional subtractive machining. These hybrid processes allow complex internal structures to be built additively and then finished with high-precision CNC cutting, making them ideal for lightweight aerospace components and customized medical implants. Human–Machine Collaboration and Augmented Reality Future CNC environments will emphasize human–machine collaboration, where operators work alongside intelligent machining systems rather than simply monitoring them. Augmented reality (AR) tools will support setup, training, and maintenance by overlaying digital instructions directly onto physical machinery. Technicians wearing AR headsets will be guided step-by-step through complex calibration or repair processes, reducing training time and lowering the risk of error. Furthermore, virtual simulation environments will allow engineers to preview machining operations before any material is cut. This not only helps validate designs but also ensures that tooling and fixturing are optimized for efficiency and safety. Conclusion Summary of Key Benefits CNC technology has transformed modern manufacturing by improving precision, efficiency, and flexibility. It enables complex machining, reduces errors, and accelerates production cycles. Impact on Modern Manufacturing With industrial CNC technology, advanced machines, and comprehensive services, manufacturers can achieve high-quality output, innovate rapidly, and maintain a competitive edge. As CNC technology continues to evolve, its influence on the manufacturing industry will only grow stronger. Be Part of the PCBWay 7th Project Design Contest! by: PCBWay Sep 03,2024 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News We are glad to announce that PCBWay 7th Project Design Contest has arrived. Prior to this, PCBWay successfully held six design contests. In each contest, we saw many eye-catching projects shared by outstanding and creative electronic engineers and enthusiasts. PCBWay 7th Project Design Contest will continue the previous purpose, which is to encourage more and more people to explore the charm of electronic design and participate in it. PCBWay 7th Project Design Contest: https://www.pcbway.com/activity/7th-project-design-contest.html . In this contest, in addition to the two themes of Electronic Project and Mechanical Project that have appeared before, we also introduced STM32 Project, hoping to give designers more room to perform. The contest will start on September 2nd, 2024, and project submissions will be accepted until January 19th, 2025. After this, the judging phase will begin, and the final winners will be announced on the PCBWay Blog on March 10th, 2025. Two ways to participate in the contest: Go to the contest page, find the Participate Now button and click it. In this case, the submitted project will automatically be entered into the competition; participants only need to select the theme of entry. Please note that if you are submitting a mechanical project, please switch to the CNC |3D Printing Project page. After filling in all the project information, simply click "Submit" at the bottom of the page. Go to the SharedProject Community ( https://www.pcbway.com/project/shareproject/ ) and click Create a project. Select the theme you are going to participate in. Similarly, if you are submitting a mechanical project, please switch to the CNC |3D Printing Project page. Hint: Sharing complete project files, including Gerber, BOM, Centroid file, schematics, 3D files, and so on will increase the chances of receiving a higher score. Awards and corresponding prizes: The First Prize : 1 winner, $1500 Cash + $200 Coupon + A Palm-sized Robot Dog*1 The Second Prize : 2 winners, $1000 Cash + $100 Coupon + Raspberry Pi 5 4GB *1 The Third Prize : 3 winners, $500 Cash + $50 Coupon + OpenMV4 H7 R2 Cam Smart Camera *1 Popular Design Prize : 10 winners, $100 Cash + $20 Coupon + $10 3D Printing Coupon + Multimeter ZTY890DPro *1 Participation Prize : Raspberry Pi Pico * 1 STM32 Great Project Prize : Six-Claw Multifunctional Aluminum Alloy Soldering Table *1 For more detailed information about the contest, please refer to: https://www.pcbway.com/activity/7th-project-design-contest.html . If there are any questions or suggestions, feel free to leave a comment below.We wish you the best of luck and look forward to your innovative designs! Verify Now Blog > Corporate Social Responsibility of PCBWay Corporate Social Responsibility of PCBWay by: PCBWay May 30,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News PCBWay recognizes the significant role it plays within the supply chain and broader society, along with the potential impact of its operations. To this end, we have established and strictly enforce the following principles, which not only govern our own conduct but also set clear expectations for our partners. Our goal is to ensure full legal and regulatory compliance, promote long-term sustainability, and generate a positive impact on society. Human Rights and Labor Protection No employment of individuals below the legal working age; all forms of forced or bonded labor are strictly prohibited. Discrimination and harassment in the workplace are not tolerated; an inclusive work environment for persons with disabilities is encouraged. Employees must be provided with fair compensation and reasonable rest periods, and their rights to freedom of association and collective bargaining must be respected. Business Ethics and Compliance Offering, promising, soliciting, or accepting any form of bribery is strictly prohibited; effective conflict of interest management and whistleblowing mechanisms must be in place. All financial and business records must accurately, completely, and truthfully reflect the underlying transactions. Full compliance with international sanctions, export controls, and other applicable laws and regulations is required. Supply Chain Responsibility and Sustainable Procurement PCBWay and its partners are required to extend the principles outlined in this document to all levels of entities within the supply chain. Priority should be given to selecting partners that are legally compliant, socially responsible, and committed to sustainable development. Identify social, labor, and environmental risks related to operations, and develop corresponding control and mitigation measures. Encourage partners to prioritize local sourcing to support regional economic development and job creation. Environmental Protection and Workplace Safety Actively implement environmental protection measures and continuously promote energy conservation and emission reduction; Ensure that all waste and hazardous materials are disposed of in accordance with relevant laws and regulations. The procurement or use of prohibited materials is not allowed. Provide employees with a safe working environment and health support mechanisms to prevent occupational injuries and health risks. PCBWay has fully adopted the DHL GoGreen transportation service in 2025 to reduce carbon emissions in the supply chain and promote the development of a green supply chain, with an initial target of reducing emissions by 30%. Information Protection and Transparent Governance Establish a comprehensive security system to strictly protect the confidentiality of customer data, drawings, and other business information. Comply with relevant laws and regulations to safeguard the personal data of customers and employees. Ensure that financial records are true, accurate, and complete, and prohibit any illegal activities. PCBWay will ensure the implementation of the above principles in actual cooperation and reserves the right to take action against any violations. To this end, we have established and strictly enforce the following principles, which not only govern our own conduct but also set clear expectations for our partners. Our goal is to ensure full legal and regulatory compliance, promote long-term sustainability, and generate a positive impact on society. Human Rights and Labor Protection No employment of individuals below the legal working age; all forms of forced or bonded labor are strictly prohibited. Discrimination and harassment in the workplace are not tolerated; an inclusive work environment for persons with disabilities is encouraged. Employees must be provided with fair compensation and reasonable rest periods, and their rights to freedom of association and collective bargaining must be respected. Business Ethics and Compliance Offering, promising, soliciting, or accepting any form of bribery is strictly prohibited; effective conflict of interest management and whistleblowing mechanisms must be in place. All financial and business records must accurately, completely, and truthfully reflect the underlying transactions. Full compliance with international sanctions, export controls, and other applicable laws and regulations is required. Supply Chain Responsibility and Sustainable Procurement PCBWay and its partners are required to extend the principles outlined in this document to all levels of entities within the supply chain. Priority should be given to selecting partners that are legally compliant, socially responsible, and committed to sustainable development. Identify social, labor, and environmental risks related to operations, and develop corresponding control and mitigation measures. Encourage partners to prioritize local sourcing to support regional economic development and job creation. Environmental Protection and Workplace Safety Actively implement environmental protection measures and continuously promote energy conservation and emission reduction; Ensure that all waste and hazardous materials are disposed of in accordance with relevant laws and regulations. The procurement or use of prohibited materials is not allowed. Provide employees with a safe working environment and health support mechanisms to prevent occupational injuries and health risks. PCBWay has fully adopted the DHL GoGreen transportation service in 2025 to reduce carbon emissions in the supply chain and promote the development of a green supply chain, with an initial target of reducing emissions by 30%. Information Protection and Transparent Governance Establish a comprehensive security system to strictly protect the confidentiality of customer data, drawings, and other business information. Comply with relevant laws and regulations to safeguard the personal data of customers and employees. Ensure that financial records are true, accurate, and complete, and prohibit any illegal activities. PCBWay will ensure the implementation of the above principles in actual cooperation and reserves the right to take action against any violations. However, DHL’s customs declaration system may inaccurately apply or fail to recognize the 125% exemption. If the recipient finds that the product is indeed eligible for the exemption but the 125% duty relief was not applied, they must file a dispute with DHL immediately, as there is a strict deadline for appeals. By the time the sender notices the issue, the appeal window may have already closed. Note: Regarding why your social security number/tax ID number/IRS number/importer number is needed when shipping, please check out this official article for explanation: Why is an overseas supplier asking for my social security number/tax ID number/IRS number/importer number? ============================================================================================== by the way： Importers - Why is an overseas supplier asking for my social security number/tax ID number/IRS number/importer number? When an individual or company purchases goods from an overseas supplier, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) considers them the ultimate importer. The ultimate importer can clear the goods or have a Customs Broker clear them on their behalf. If the supplier hires a carrier that provides door to door service, the carrier service usually has brokers in their supply chain to clear the goods on behalf of the ultimate importer. If a formal entry is required, CBP regulations require the broker to put the ultimate importer's identification number on the CBP Form 7501- Entry Summary. The ultimate importer's identification number is either the Employers Identification Number (EIN) tax identification number assigned by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) or the importer's social security number. The EIN is issued for the purpose of tax administration and are not intended for participation in any other activities (e.g., tax lien auction or sales, lotteries). For additional information about EIN, please visit the IRS web page "Apply for an Employer Identification (EIN) Online." Goods are usually cleared informally when they are for personal use, under $2500 in value, and are not in commercial quantities. A formal entry is usually required for commercial importations valued over $2,500. Because many foreign merchants are aware that CBP requires an identification number for the ultimate importer for formal entries, they will often request the purchaser's social security number to include on export documents that the broker will subsequently rely on to prepare the CBP entry. It should be noted that paperwork for goods sent by courier service does ask for an importer number, whether the import qualifies for an informal entry or not. Courier services file CBP entries electronically, and the software system they use requires an identification number to be provided for the recipient of the goods. If an identification number is not provided, the courier service is required to file a paper entry, which is extremely time-consuming and in the world of "Overnight Delivery" not practical. The end result is that most courier services will not accept packages for international delivery to U.S. residents if a recipient's identification number is not provided by the shipper. Goods sent through the international postal service that are under $2500 in value generally do not require an importer number to be cleared through CBP. It’s Trickier Than You Think. But because of an ever-changing patchwork of trade rules, not every product will be charged an astronomical tariff, trade lawyers, customs brokers and importers say. In some cases, tariffs will pile on other tariffs. In other instances, they can reduce costs, while other times they can cancel out new ones. The new 125 percent rate that President Trump imposed will in many cases be added on top of long-existing duties. There are four main categories of tariffs that are imposed on goods from China. Note: The tariff on auto parts comes into effect in early May. The average provided for the base rate is calculated by the World Trade Organization, which computes an average of all tariff lines. A large share of U.S. imports are assigned a 0% duty, but there are some very high rates in the tariff schedule. Rates ultimately depend on what is imported, what materials are used (from where), which special rates are applied and what sorts of products are exempt. Note: Regarding why your social security number/tax ID number/IRS number/importer number is needed when shipping, please check out this official article for explanation: Why is an overseas supplier asking for my social security number/tax ID number/IRS number/importer number? ============================================================================================== by the way： Importers - Why is an overseas supplier asking for my social security number/tax ID number/IRS number/importer number? When an individual or company purchases goods from an overseas supplier, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) considers them the ultimate importer. The ultimate importer can clear the goods or have a Customs Broker clear them on their behalf. If the supplier hires a carrier that provides door to door service, the carrier service usually has brokers in their supply chain to clear the goods on behalf of the ultimate importer. If a formal entry is required, CBP regulations require the broker to put the ultimate importer's identification number on the CBP Form 7501- Entry Summary. The ultimate importer's identification number is either the Employers Identification Number (EIN) tax identification number assigned by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) or the importer's social security number. The EIN is issued for the purpose of tax administration and are not intended for participation in any other activities (e.g., tax lien auction or sales, lotteries). For additional information about EIN, please visit the IRS web page "Apply for an Employer Identification (EIN) Online." Goods are usually cleared informally when they are for personal use, under $2500 in value, and are not in commercial quantities. A formal entry is usually required for commercial importations valued over $2,500. Because many foreign merchants are aware that CBP requires an identification number for the ultimate importer for formal entries, they will often request the purchaser's social security number to include on export documents that the broker will subsequently rely on to prepare the CBP entry. It should be noted that paperwork for goods sent by courier service does ask for an importer number, whether the import qualifies for an informal entry or not. Courier services file CBP entries electronically, and the software system they use requires an identification number to be provided for the recipient of the goods. If an identification number is not provided, the courier service is required to file a paper entry, which is extremely time-consuming and in the world of "Overnight Delivery" not practical. The end result is that most courier services will not accept packages for international delivery to U.S. residents if a recipient's identification number is not provided by the shipper. Goods sent through the international postal service that are under $2500 in value generally do not require an importer number to be cleared through CBP. It’s Trickier Than You Think. But because of an ever-changing patchwork of trade rules, not every product will be charged an astronomical tariff, trade lawyers, customs brokers and importers say. In some cases, tariffs will pile on other tariffs. In other instances, they can reduce costs, while other times they can cancel out new ones. Since the first exhibition was held in 1964, electronica has gradually grown and now covers the entire world of electronics, including the micro- and nano-worlds of semiconductor and micro systems technology, as well as measurement and sensor technology, display technology and vehicle electronics, etc., which is the best choice for any technology enthusiasts and industry practitioners. PCBWay has participated in theelectronica many times and has received a warm response every time. At the exhibition, everyone has the opportunity to get close to our various products and fully evaluate the performance and quality of our products, which is far beyond the scope of online communication. On-site interaction gives us the opportunity to answer everyone's questions in a timely manner and help them understand the products more comprehensively, thereby accelerating the process of cooperation. Therefore, after the exhibition, we not only strengthened our cooperation with existing customers, but also successfully attracted the attention of many new potential partners. This new product has attracted the attention and interest of many customers, so we hope to take this opportunity to let everyone experience the excellent effect and quality of the color-printed board in person. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Fabrication Toolkit for Kicad PCBWay Fabrication Toolkit for Kicad by: PCBWay Oct 11,2023 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News Recently, PCBWay added a plug-in called PCBWay Fabrication Toolkit to Kicad: With just one click of the mouse, four files can be exported from the layout file automatically: Gerber file, IPC-Netlist file, BOM file and Pick and Place file, which can significantly improves the efficiency of pre-production work. Installation from the Official KiCad Repositories After installation, the plugin will appear on the right side of the navigation bar. And users can use it to export all the production files with just a click. Process demonstration： Sending the files to PCBWay, and they can be used for production after being reviewed by the staff. Note: If you want to place an assembly order, please be sure to add MPN information to the BOM. This can help the quoter source the devices you need more accurately. Manual installation Except for the way mentioned before, you can also download the latest ZIP file from https://github.com/pcbway/PCBWay-Fabrication-Toolkit-for-KiCad: Open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the main window of KiCad and install the ZIP file via "Install from File". About BOM Through BOM files, we can get all information of the components used in your design. In order to speed up the quotation process, we need this information: 1. Designator (necessary) 2. Quantity (necessary) 3. MPN/Part Number (necessary) 4. Package/Footprint (necessary) 5. Manufacturer (optional) 6. Description/value (optional) If you have more suggestions, please leave a message below, PCBWay has committed to providing everyone with high-quality services. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad by: Anson Apr 01,2022 Posted in News Kicad PCB design Send your layout to PCBWay for instant production with just one click. Have you ever thought that when you complete the design on KiCad, you can place an order on pcbway with just one click? Now this idea is finally achieved (it's not an April Fool's joke). When you click PCBWay Plug-in button on Kicad, we will export these files in your project ( Please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin released at 2026 )： 1.Gerber files in correct format for production 2.IPC-Netlist file 3.Bom-file that includes all information of components 4.Pick and Place-file used in assembly You can click "Save to Cart" to place an order immediately after uploading the files( usually only takes a few seconds), our engineers will double check the files before the production. Note:We have updated plugin for Kicad 10,you could also place assembly order directly now. But we need to get the component "Manufacture Part Number". Please confirm you run the "Update Board from Schematic" and install the latest version of the plugin. ﻿ Installation from the official KiCad repositories Just open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the KiCad main menu an install the "PCBWay Plug-in for KiCad" plugin from the selection list. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad by: Anson Apr 01,2022 Posted in News Kicad PCB design Send your layout to PCBWay for instant production with just one click. Have you ever thought that when you complete the design on KiCad, you can place an order on pcbway with just one click? Now this idea is finally achieved (it's not an April Fool's joke). When you click PCBWay Plug-in button on Kicad, we will export these files in your project ( Please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin released at 2026 )： 1.Gerber files in correct format for production 2.IPC-Netlist file 3.Bom-file that includes all information of components 4.Pick and Place-file used in assembly You can click "Save to Cart" to place an order immediately after uploading the files( usually only takes a few seconds), our engineers will double check the files before the production. Note:We have updated plugin for Kicad 10,you could also place assembly order directly now. But we need to get the component "Manufacture Part Number". Please confirm you run the "Update Board from Schematic" and install the latest version of the plugin. ﻿ Installation from the official KiCad repositories Just open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the KiCad main menu an install the "PCBWay Plug-in for KiCad" plugin from the selection list. Manual installation You can also download the latest ZIP file from https://github.com/pcbway/PCBWay-Plug-in-for-Kicad , then open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the main window of KiCad and install the ZIP file via "Install from File". About Bom We can get all information of components used in your design ( please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin) . In order to speed up the quotation of components, we need this information: 1. Designator (necessary) 2. Quantity (necessary) 3. MPN/Part Number (necessary) 4. Package/Footprint (necessary) 5. Manufacturer (optional) 6. Description/value (optional) You just need to add the properties in your schematic like the picture shows: As a sponsor of KiCad, we will always support its development.
